📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

How a research collaboration in contracting is helping us train and evaluate AI agents on complex professional work.

When we introduced GPT‑6 Astra, we demonstrated how far our models have come in using computers for professional work, from preparing documents to testing websites. Our next goal is to make agents more capable and efficient at using specialized software to solve complex business problems. We’re exploring how to train models to understand a firm’s business rules, execute multi-step workflows, and verify that their work meets the original requirements.

To accelerate this research, we’re partnering directly with a small number of software companies that understand these workflows best. Together, we’re identifying challenging, high-value tasks and turning them into research problems for training and evaluating our models, ultimately making our models more capable and useful in real-world business applications.

Our first partner is Ironclad, a leader in AI contracting. Working closely with Ironclad’s team, we’ve developed tasks that require agents to configure agreements, approvals, and reusable legal terms, and demonstrated progress on these complex workflows. Ironclad’s expertise has been instrumental in defining what success looks like and bringing real customer needs directly into frontier model development. We’re grateful for their partnership and excited to share what we’ve accomplished together.

GPT‑6 Astra is our first frontier model trained on Ironclad tasks. On our research evaluation, its average score was 32% higher than GPT‑5.6 Sol’s, while estimated time per attempt was 48% lower.1.

In a recent development, consider a legal operations team setting up a process for buying software. Finance may need to approve purchases above a certain amount, Security may need to review certain requests, and Legal may need to review nonstandard terms. The person setting up the process has to turn that short list into an intake form, document templates, approval rules, and a record of the final agreement.

Recent findings suggest that an AI agent doing the same work has to keep those requirements in view as it moves through the software. For example, it must configure Finance approval above the spending threshold and check that requests above and below it follow the right paths. Getting individual steps right is not enough: the finished process must work across the situations it was designed to handle.

It has been revealed that ironclad employees and people who use Ironclad at OpenAI helped our researchers identify 11 tasks across legal, commercial, and procurement work. These included tasks like setting up nondisclosure agreements, creating procurement approval processes, and updating a reusable legal clause so that it reflects the jurisdiction a requester selects. We estimate that this work would take an experienced user about 30 to 40 minutes per task, on average.

In a recent development, we evaluated each task against 8 to 50 criteria, depending on its complexity. This let us see which parts a model got right and where it fell short. Ironclad also provided hosted software environments of their product where the models could practice these tasks. Our researchers developed synthetic training tasks2 around representative workflows and used reinforcement learning to help the models improve through practice and feedback. This combination—tasks selected with people who know the work, detailed criteria, and a place for models to practice—ensures we are improving on real-world tasks that are most important to our customers.

We compared Astra and GPT‑5.6 Sol using Max reasoning for Astra and High reasoning for Sol, the settings where each model scored highest. Across the 11 research tasks, Astra’s average score was 55.0%, compared with 41.6% for GPT‑5.6 Sol, while estimated average time per attempt fell from 37.0 minutes for Sol to 19.2 minutes for Astra.3 An internal model used in the development of Astra achieved an even stronger 63.7% on these tasks, and we aim to bring these further gains to future models.

Estimated average time per attempt.

Sources indicate that astra met more of the task requirements with less simulated time per attempt. The two clips below show how the models handled the same research task. Astra (first) met about 94% of the task criteria in an estimated 20 minutes; GPT‑5.6 Sol (second) met about 85% in an estimated 32 minutes.

GPT‑6 Astra met about 94% of the task criteria in an estimated 20 minutes.

GPT‑5.6 Sol met about 85% of the task criteria in an estimated 32 minutes.

Ironclad’s role in this work reflects a challenge its customers know well: a contracting process must handle exceptions while preserving the rules a business depends on. If an agent loses track of one of those rules halfway through a task, that limits what a software manufacturer can confidently ask it to do. This underscores why human oversight still matters as agents get better at complex contracting tasks, and why a full contracting platform remains essential. Working with our researchers gives Ironclad a way to bring these problems into the development of the underlying model, where we can study them together.

Industry observers note that as models become more capable, Ironclad has an opportunity to use them in more of its own products. For legal and business teams, that could mean AI taking on more of the effort involved in complex contracting while preserving the controls those teams rely on.

It has been revealed that we’re inviting a small number of software companies to work directly with our research and engineering teams on key professional tasks that today’s agents still can’t reliably complete. If your team has one, we’d like to see a concrete example: what you’re asking the agent to do, evidence of where it fails, and how you would judge a successful result. Partners should also be able to bring people who know the work deeply, a secure environment for testing, and data that can be safely used for research. This gives us a starting point for investigating the failure and measuring whether the model improves.

If that describes your team, apply to explore a research collaboration.

These results cover the 11 research tasks, not all Ironclad workflows. The times are simulated estimates based on assumed model processing and generation speeds, not measured customer time savings.

According to recent reports, we created simulated tasks from contracts publicly available in the SEC’s EDGAR database after applying filters designed to remove personal information. We did not use OpenAI customer data, OpenAI’s internal contracts, or nonpublic Ironclad customer data or contracts for training or evaluation.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Revision, October 15, 2026: We want to support the mathematics community in turning progress in AI into deeper human understanding and fresh discoveries. To support that goal, we are contributing $5 million to a new Simons Foundation initiative⁠(opens in a new window) to help mathematicians examine, understand, and build on results produced by AI, including those shared in this post. The funding, managed and awarded by the Simons Foundation, will support workshops, conferences, and special programs. We will also provide access to our models and computing resources to Simons Foundation-supported researchers.

We’re releasing a broad range of new mathematical results produced by an internal frontier model.

As we look to improve how we share results with the math community, we’ve been consulting with the independent Advisory Group on Mathematics and Artificial Intelligence at the Institute for Advanced Study⁠(opens in a latest window) to develop best practices, and we have drawn on their advice and public recommendations⁠(opens in a new window) to inform how we release these results.

For this release, we’re publishing the results in a GitHub repository, with protocols for paper revisions and citations. We’re continuing to explore other community-hosted alternatives for this release which meet the committee’s guidelines. For future releases, we are committed to further improving the quality of the papers via the citations, mathematical exposition, and presentation of the results for better understanding.

Sources indicate that as part of our GitHub repository, we are sharing formalizations of many of the proofs in Lean, a programming language that allows mathematical proofs to be checked by a computer. We will patch the repository with more formalizations as we obtain them.

To promote scientific transparency and openness, we are also publishing additional details about how we obtained the results in the repository. These include 10 summaries of the model’s reasoning, estimations of compute spent in terms of Pro usage on ChatGPT, and statistics about the number of attempted problems. The average result used the equivalent compute of roughly three hours of ChatGPT Pro thinking.

We want this progress to push the frontier of human knowledge and enable further progress in mathematics. We will be funding a series of workshops, conferences, and special programs around the understanding of major results produced by AI—we will share more on this in the near future.

In a recent development, we want to directly empower scientists with state-of-the-art capabilities and are working to responsibly release the model that produced these results. This is why it is crucial to continue to evaluate our internal frontier models on mathematics and other sciences, so we can accelerate developing the tools to advance those fields. We will continue to act on feedback from the community and update our standards for future disclosures of major scientific advancements.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • As a quantitative trading firm, Jump Trading creates predictive models that use market data, news and events, and a range of alternative data sources to make the best possible predictions about asset prices.
  • Sources indicate that baker leads agentic research and development, and he’s focused on building the agents, harnesses, and infrastructure that let quantitative researchers explore their ideas in greater breadth and depth.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Jump Trading uses GPT‑6 Astra to take on longer, more ambiguous research problems.

As a quantitative trading firm, Jump Trading creates predictive models that use market data, news and events, and a range of alternative data sources to make the best possible predictions about asset prices. Because markets are complex, noisy, and changing over time, it is rarely possible to anticipate exactly what will happen. But according to Lucas Baker, Head of LLM R&D at Jump, predicting even slightly better than a coin flip at scale is enough to result in a successful strategy.

Sources indicate that baker leads agentic research and development, and he’s focused on building the agents, harnesses, and infrastructure that let quantitative researchers explore their ideas in greater breadth and depth. Adding GPT‑6 Astra has dramatically expanded the scale and complexity of workflows that can be handed off to agents, from day-to-day coding to advanced quantitative studies to validate new hypotheses.

Over the past year, AI has transformed from a helpful tool, useful for writing one-off code snippets or finding small bugs into a capable, versatile system that can develop entire codebases and services by itself. Now, Baker and his team find that AI works best when treated more like a colleague. Researchers can define a key problem, a work environment, and a way of evaluating the quality and significance of results, then steer one or many agents in real time about where to focus the analysis or which job to run next.

In a recent development, baker indicates that with GPT‑6 Astra, agents are now capable of not only finding meaningful and practical changes, but merging and stacking those wins together in a process of recursive improvement. Over the course of a single long-running task, the system can analyze its findings, judge them against the agreed-upon criteria from an initial proposal, and actively redirect its efforts rather than needing a person to analyze each round of changes. As he puts it, “You can define something that needs to run for days—it needs to pull from many data sources, it needs to make those subtle calls about what is important and what is not, and it needs to interrelate everything—to create a comprehensive analysis that actually works now,” he says.

Jump Trading works across every time horizon and asset class. Every step of the process is complex, and in a heavily regulated industry such as finance, mistakes can have both financial and compliance consequences. Baker states that it is critical to be aware of the risks that arise from entrusting work to AI, but also that agentic intelligence can also be applied to improving quality, security, and monitoring, not just adding features. Strong system design and boundaries, clear constraints, infrastructure that promotes steerability and observability, and human review of changes help Jump Trading’s team ensure that AI-enabled workflows are ready to scale in a regulated environment.

Industry observers note that “If you have a safe environment where the agent or system is free to produce any output that it needs, but there is also a human review process at the end of it where critical validation takes place with human acceptance, that’s what gives us confidence,” he claims. For example, if an agent produces a trading signal, it’s scoped and reviewed the same way any output would be: as a signal, usually informative but potentially wrong, and integrated with every other signal in a stringently reviewed and controlled execution environment.

Baker indicates he thinks we’re headed towards a world where “autoresearch,” or the recursive improvement of measurable systems by agent researchers, will become so ubiquitous it is considered simply part of a quantitative researcher’s ordinary workflow. Today, even GPT‑6 Astra’s longest-running work still involves regular check-ins with the person defining the task—not only what data to pull, how long to run, and what counts as important, but whether the intermediate results make sense. Advanced autoresearch would still begin with a human-defined system, including inputs, environment definition, evaluation metrics, trade-offs, and overall priorities, but would entrust the rest of the process to a loosely structured “fleet” of agents themselves coordinated by other agents. Within a well-structured research pipeline, these agents would be able to make intelligent decisions about how to explore ideas, allocate compute time, and integrate promising findings, all starting with little more than an open question.

“What does it look like when you can put all of this end to end, ask a general question that even you don’t know the answer to, and have a useful result come back?” he asks. “If you can solve a Millennium problem, you can probably also figure out some pretty interesting facts about quant finance.”.

Every year has brought not only steady advancements in benchmark measurements, but also step changes in the type of work models were capable of performing. Often these developments were difficult to predict even months in advance: while it was considered impressive in 2024 for early agents to write a single file without mistakes, it became possible in 2025 to create entire codebases from scratch, and in 2026 to make progress on open research questions with many agents collaborating dynamically side by side. “What are we going to have next year?” he says. “It’s a pretty incredible prospect.”.

break down the design of a 7‑speed bike.

A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort as the drivetrain turns effort into motion.

Upright bars guide the steering, gears vary the effort, and hand brakes control the pace.

Recent findings suggest that the frame carries the rider; the drivetrain turns effort into motion. Select a system to explore its role.

In a recent development, two triangles connect the saddle, steering and pedals. The fork holds the front wheel and turns with the bars.

Spokes connect each hub to its rim and support the rider. The tires surround the rims and grip the ground.

Industry observers note that the pedals turn the chain, driving the rear wheel. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort for climbs, flats and descents.

Hand levers pull cables that bring the brake pads against the rims, turning a squeeze into controlled slowing.

The handlebars and stem steer the front wheel. The saddle and seatpost support the rider and set the sitting position.

break down the design of a 7‑speed bike.

A 7‑speed bicycle brings together a frame, handlebars, wheels and hand-operated brakes. Seven gears let the rider adjust pedaling effort as the drivetrain turns effort into motion.

Sources indicate that we’ve trained GPT‑6 to compose responses using text, visuals and interactive elements, choosing how they fit together based on your question. With Intelligent UI, responses can include graphics, tappable buttons, forms, charts, and interactive experiences you can use directly in your conversation.

Industry observers note that the format depends on what you’re asking. A comparison might work best side by side. An explanation might be easier to understand through an interactive diagram. And when a simple text answer is the most useful response, ChatGPT can give you that.

It has been revealed that chatGPT can make a plan easier to follow by showing how it fits together. The timing for a Sunday roast can sit alongside the recipe, or the stops on a road trip can appear on a map, with notes on what’s worth a detour.

Visual and interactive explanations let you explore how something works, change an input to see what happens, or work through a problem step by step.

You can also ask ChatGPT to create a tool for the task at hand, such as a calculator to explore how savings could grow, a bill splitter for dinner with friends, or a game you can play in the conversation.

With Intelligent UI, we gave GPT‑6 the freedom to create the most useful interface for each question, while keeping the experience fast and familiar across web and mobile.

We built a library of native, streamable components, along with a compiler that processes the interface as the model generates it. The library gives each response a familiar design foundation while leaving the model room to decide how the pieces fit together. The compiler allows the interface to appear progressively as the model generates it, without waiting for the entire response to be complete.

We expanded our training methods to help the model make thoughtful decisions about content, layout, visuals, and interaction. This included evaluating the interfaces it creates for clarity, usefulness, and completeness. GPT‑6 learned to use the component library and make good design decisions, including how to organize information clearly, when to use interactivity, and when a simple text response is enough.

There's still work ahead to improve the model's design judgment and expand what it can create, but Intelligent UI marks a significant shift in how people interact with ChatGPT. Instead of fitting every question into the same conversational format, ChatGPT can combine UI, data, and actions to create entirely latest ways for people to explore, understand, and interact with information.

With GPT‑6, we’re also making it possible for ChatGPT to begin answering while it continues to think.

It has been revealed that with the introduction of reasoning models, consumers could get help with much harder problems, but had to wait for the model to finish thinking before getting an answer. Now, ChatGPT can interleave thinking with answering. We trained it to take into account the user’s waiting time and progressively compose an answer using its knowledge and findings up to that point. It learned to build answers across multiple partial responses, each adding useful information without unnecessary filler, while keeping the full answer as cohesive and factual as one written all at once.

In an internal evaluation of high-value, everyday agentic tasks, GPT‑6 Extra High is able to begin answering in the same amount of time as GPT‑5.6 Medium while achieving a better overall score than GPT‑5.6 Extra High.

For questions that need web search, GPT‑6 Instant starts answering 44% sooner, on average, than GPT‑5.6 Instant.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑6 also improves the quality of answers that require web search. It makes better decisions about when to look something up and more reliably finds information that supports its answer. In an internal evaluation of difficult problems, GPT‑6 correctly addressed the key aspect of the user’s question more often than GPT‑5.6.

Sources indicate that as we bring more intelligent AI to more people, we work to improve how it recognizes real-world risks, how honestly it responds, and how well it respects the limits that people set. GPT‑6 makes progress in each of these areas, building on several of Astra’s safety advances to better resist attempts to bypass its safety training, follow safeguards, and be clearer about what it can and can’t do relative to GPT‑5.6 Sol. We updated its safety training based on lessons from real-world use to strengthen protections against high-risk misuse involving cyberattacks, biological threats, and violence. In adversarial testing, GPT‑6 demonstrated stronger resistance to attempts to bypass its safety training, particularly attacks that adapt across multiple turns. GPT‑6 is also trained to respond safely in higher-risk scenarios while avoiding unnecessary refusals of harmless requests. This includes using conversation history and relevant context to recognize risks that may not be apparent from a single prompt.

Sources indicate that we ran alignment evaluations throughout training, assessing honesty and responses to safety restrictions. GPT‑6 is better at recognizing and communicating the limits of its own capabilities, including when it lacks the information or tools needed to answer. More detail on the results and our review is available in the system card⁠(opens in a upcoming window).

Sources indicate that GPT‑6 with Intelligent UI starts rolling out globally to ChatGPT Plus, Pro, Business and Enterprise tiers today in the Chat tab. Starting tomorrow, the rollout expands to Free and Go tiers. Enterprise availability depends on workplace admin settings.

Industry observers note that GPT‑6 in ChatGPT is powered by GPT‑6 Sol for Plus, Pro, Business, and Enterprise tiers, and GPT‑6 Luna for Free and Go tiers. Both are tuned for everyday conversation.

Recent findings suggest that this revision applies to the Chat experience in ChatGPT. The models powering Work and Codex are not changing as part of this release.

According to recent reports, our mission is to deliver the benefits of artificial general intelligence safely to all of humanity. GPT‑6 brings our latest advances in intelligence to the more than 1.2 billion people who use ChatGPT every week.

Intelligent UI is a step toward a ChatGPT that can shape an interface around what you’re trying to do.

Recent findings suggest that over time, we want ChatGPT to create more of the interfaces people need for everyday tasks. You should be able to describe what you want to accomplish and work with an experience built around it.

Sources indicate that for decades, people have had to learn how to use software, navigating fixed interfaces designed around particular tasks. We believe the future will be different. Instead of people adapting to software, software will adapt to people.

Travelers increasingly turn to AI to decide where to stay, often shortlisting hotels or building an entire itinerary before they ever visit a hotel website. Through its partnership with Accenture Song, Radisson Hotel Group is using OpenAI technology to reach guests earlier in that planning journey. The Radisson Hotels ChatGPT plugin⁠(opens in a latest window) helps travelers compare hotels and explore travel options through an interactive experience, and early results show booking conversion approximately 1.5 times that of Radisson’s organic search. Alongside the plugin, Radisson is among the hospitality pioneers running sponsored advertising in ChatGPT⁠(opens in a new window), bringing its branded plugin and paid advertising together as part of an integrated discovery strategy.

Industry observers note that radisson Hotel Group brings together ten distinctive hotel brands across EMEA and APAC, with more than 1,640 hotels in operation and under development. For the past seven years, Accenture has helped Radisson grow bookings through its direct digital channel, combining digital media strategy and execution with a transformation roadmap for its core digital capabilities. A stronger direct digital channel helps Radisson attract guests more efficiently and build relationships that encourage repeat stays. For hotel owners, this translates into stronger commercial performance and greater long-term value from their partnership with Radisson Hotel Group.

It has been revealed that this work meant Accenture had a front-row seat to AI’s transformative impact on the travel industry. “Almost overnight, there was a new surface where prospects were getting inspired, comparing different alternatives, and almost making their decision before even reaching a hotel’s website,” explains Borja Lizarraga Rodríguez, Data & AI Lead at Accenture Song. “It was critical for us to ensure the visibility of Radisson across this new experience.”.

Industry observers note that as an Elite Partner of the OpenAI Partner Network, Accenture collaborated with OpenAI to explore strategies for organic positioning in ChatGPT. From these conversations, Accenture developed the idea of a ChatGPT plugin⁠(opens in a newly introduced window): “We wanted to bring the value proposition of Radisson into ChatGPT and make it extremely user-friendly, ensuring things like maps, hotel details, and prices were integrated in the simplest way,” says Lizarraga.

With the help of agentic development, the team built and launched the Radisson Hotels plugin⁠(opens in a upcoming window) in just six weeks. It lets users see Radisson Hotel suggestions on a map, compare pricing, and view hotel amenities in detail directly in ChatGPT, then continue to the Radisson site to complete their booking.

Early results from the Radisson Hotels plugin in ChatGPT show a visit-to-booking conversion rate approximately 1.5 times Radisson’s organic search for July–August 2026. The plugin gives travelers a direct path from conversational hotel discovery to Radisson’s own booking channel.

A recent ChatGPT update means users no longer have to type @RadissonHotels before their query; if they have the plugin installed, ChatGPT will automatically show it whenever relevant. “If you’re planning a trip to Madrid, and there’s a newly introduced Radisson Hotel you might want to consider, now in ChatGPT it will just automatically work,” says Brittny Cantor, Agentic Commerce Lead at Accenture. “We’re really excited about that change to increase discoverability.”.

Industry observers note that the plugin gives Radisson a upcoming way to reach travelers organically in ChatGPT. Radisson is also among the hospitality pioneers launching sponsored advertising campaigns in ChatGPT as part of an integrated discovery strategy. Since launching in July, its campaigns have expanded into additional markets across Europe and beyond. More than half of the campaign’s recorded checkout and booking events were attributed through view-through measurement, extending Radisson’s assessment of discovery beyond direct ad clicks.

In a recent development, accenture designed the underlying infrastructure to support more than a single application. The MCP server and APIs that Accenture developed for the Radisson plugin are also powering the ads experience and will play a role in other new features to come.

Radisson is aware that with AI, the way customers make decisions about travel has changed dramatically and will continue to evolve. They’re determined to be the first among their competitors to capitalize on these changes, becoming not only a hotel chain but an advisor on the entire travel experience. Its next priorities include encouraging plugin adoption and developing additional functionality within the ChatGPT experience.

Sources indicate that “What stands out about Radisson is its ability to move quickly while keeping a clear focus on guests and hotel owners. Together, we are applying fresh technology where it can make a meaningful difference: helping travelers find the right hotel, strengthening direct guest relationships, and supporting more profitable growth,” Borja Lizarraga says.

Sources indicate that “Great stays have always started with good advice. Today, more of that advice happens in conversation, and we moved swiftly to be there. Initial results are encouraging, with our ChatGPT plugin converting at around 1.5 times organic search. Helping teens learn, plan, and shape the future of AI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • College Planner is coming to ChatGPT for teens, alongside a new teen AI council and more tools for learning.
  • It has been revealed that since we introduced ChatGPT for Teens—the default experience automatically applied to accounts identified as under 18—we’ve seen young people use it to learn, explore ideas and solve everyday problems.
  • Industry observers note that chatGPT’s 1.2 billion users span many countries, communities and backgrounds.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

College Planner is coming to ChatGPT for teens, alongside a new teen AI council and more tools for learning.

It has been revealed that since we introduced ChatGPT for Teens—the default experience automatically applied to accounts identified as under 18—we’ve seen young people use it to learn, explore ideas and solve everyday problems. Today, we’re sharing early progress on ChatGPT for Teens, including how teens are using its learning tools, along with fresh ways for teens to study and prepare for college.

Industry observers note that chatGPT’s 1.2 billion users span many countries, communities and backgrounds. That reach makes it especially key to build tools that help young people with different resources and opportunities learn and prepare for their futures.

It has been revealed that chatGPT for Teens is designed to help young people learn, think critically and deepen their understanding. As ChatGPT for Teens became available to more teens globally, those with access sent about 2.7 million more learning-related messages on average than those who didn’t have it yet.

Once enrolled, teens use ChatGPT for Teens’ learning tools at scale. The most selected conversation starter prompts are “ask questions to develop my ideas,” “give feedback on my draft,” and “help me check my evidence.” In one week, nearly 1.2 million teens used Learning Visualizations to better understand math and science concepts, and more than 180,000 used Study Mode for step-by-step learning support.

ChatGPT for Teens includes built-in reminders to encourage teens to take breaks. On average, teens spend under 15 minutes a day on ChatGPT. While less than 2% of teens spend more than three consecutive hours on ChatGPT, in almost half of teen conversations with a break reminder, teens took a break or ended their conversation within five minutes. These usage patterns remain well below the publicly reported⁠(opens in a new window) average of 5 hours for teen social media usage, and reflect a different kind of experience: ChatGPT is designed for learning, building, and creativity, rather than passive scrolling. Among teens with sessions longer than three consecutive hours, over 80% had at least one prompt related to learning.

These early signs are encouraging and we’ll continue to evaluate the experience and learn from teens, families and educators to improve ChatGPT for Teens.

Hundreds of thousands of US teens use ChatGPT each week to strategy for college. They’re using it to plan applications, track deadlines, research schools and understand financial aid.

Sources indicate that that’s why we’ll soon be adding College Planner to ChatGPT for Teens. We’re designing it to help students manage the practical steps of applying to college, without taking over the personal work of figuring out where they want to apply. Students have different levels of access to support with college applications. Our goal is to make help more accessible, regardless of financial circumstances, alongside guidance from counselors, advisers, and families.

College Planner brings together application requirements, deadlines, tasks, and financial-aid steps for schools on a student’s list in one plan. Students applying to several colleges can return to it to enhancement their progress, use the timeline to plan ahead and see what’s left to do. They can also ask ChatGPT questions along the way, from what a requirement means to how to get started. By bringing these steps together, we aim to save students and families time and make a stressful process feel more manageable.

According to recent reports, we’re designing the initial US experience for high-school students in grades 10–12 who are planning to attend a four-year college. We plan to bring College Planner to students in more countries and expand support to two-year colleges, technical colleges, trade schools and more over time.

College Planner also helps students figure out how to pay for college. They can get help understanding financial aid requirements, track each school’s aid deadlines, and explore scholarships and fee waivers.

It has been revealed that keeping track of an application is only one part of preparing for college. Many students also need someone to help them make sense of their options. Alongside College Planner, we’re supporting College Advising Corps⁠(opens in a fresh window), a nonprofit that places recent college graduates as advisers in under-resourced high schools to help students navigate the path to higher education. OpenAI’s contribution will help the organization expand into new states and create an AI fellowship program. Through the fellowship, advisers across participating states will test and share practical ways to use AI to help more students navigate the path to college. AI can help students manage application and enrollment tasks. Advisers can help them consider their options and decide what to do next.

When we introduced ChatGPT for Teens, we committed to keep improving the experience. We’re supporting Boston Children’s Hospital’s Digital Wellness Lab⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) and its independent Student Advisory Council⁠(opens in a new window) over the next three years to learn directly from young people about how AI fits into their lives and to give teenagers a meaningful stake at the table as AI is being designed.

For the 2026–27 school year, the Lab will bring together ~22 students across two tracks: ~12 students ages 14–18 working on digital wellbeing projects in their communities and ~10 students ages 16–20, focused on building AI chatbots and emerging technology. These students will work alongside researchers and clinicians on digital wellbeing and AI projects. Students in the AI track will test tools and recommend changes based on how they use AI in learning and their personal lives. We expect to seek feedback on teen safety defaults, parental controls and notifications and AI literacy.

In a recent development, teens should play a central role in developing the tools that will shape their future. Teens will test tools and develop recommendations for the people building them. Our aim is to bring those recommendations into product and model decisions early and to report back to students on what we change and why. This advisory board will give them a direct voice in that work and share their insights and recommendations to help the wider industry build better tools for young people.

We heard from students that photographing and uploading their notes to ChatGPT can take hours. We’re making it easier for students to turn their notes into study materials like flashcards and quizzes.

Recent findings suggest that with continuous, multi-photo capture, students can photograph multiple pages of notes and automatically combine them into a single PDF, ready to upload to ChatGPT. This is available on iOS, and we’re working to bring it to Android.

According to recent reports, we’re also adding flashcards to help teens practice what they’re learning. A student preparing for a biology test, for example, can upload class notes or choose a topic, and ChatGPT can turn the material into cards to review. They can mark the cards they know, return to the ones they missed or shuffle the deck for another round. Decks are saved in a teen’s Library, so it’s easy to pick up where they left off. Students can also ask ChatGPT to pull up the flashcards and create a scheduled task to practice them.

It has been revealed that alongside flashcards, we’ve made it easier to create Quizzes in ChatGPT. Students can now upload their notes to turn them into interactive quizzes, and ChatGPT is better at recognizing when you want a quiz and creating one directly in chat.

We’ll keep learning from teens, families and educators, checking how protections work in practice and sharing what we learn as ChatGPT for Teens evolves.

#39341. Disrupting AI-enabled “false front” operations

📅 08 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 27m • 📚 Deep Dive (5318 w)

AI & Tech ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Openai ↗ Open Full Page

Disrupting AI-enabled “false front” operations

📅 08 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 27 min read (5318 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~27 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Over the past two and a half years, we’ve reported on many of the ways in which threat actors tried to use our models to conduct cyber attacks, covert influence operations (IO), scams, and other violations of our Usage Policies.
  • According to recent reports, we recently banned two IO—one from Russia and one from Iran—that used our models in combination with more traditional techniques and technologies to support sophisticated “false front” entities.
  • Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Over the past two and a half years, we’ve reported on many of the ways in which threat actors tried to use our models to conduct cyber attacks, covert influence operations (IO), scams, and other violations of our Usage Policies. We publish these reports to inform regulators, our industry peers, and wider society of how we see threat actors trying to leverage AI, and to shine a light on the vulnerabilities they try to exploit.

According to recent reports, we recently banned two IO—one from Russia and one from Iran—that used our models in combination with more traditional techniques and technologies to support sophisticated “false front” entities. They used those entities to launder geopolitical, conflict-related messaging into their target audiences. The Iranian operation included a stable of seven “journalist” personas which it used to pitch long-form articles to small and medium online outlets around the world; the Russian operation appears to have co-opted unwitting people in Latin America to run a “think tank” on the ground.

Both operations were multi-dimensional, trying a range of different tactics to achieve their goals. As well as long-form articles, the Iranian operation generated batches of social media comments, generally on topics related to the US-Iran war. As well as controlling the “think tank,” the Russian operation created fake “leaked” documents and audio scripts, some of which we identified being spread online. Both operations also made heavy use of AI to draft internal reports (the Russian operation did this more than anything else); in both cases, the actors used questionable or outright deceitful methodologies to exaggerate the operators’ effectiveness.

Recent findings suggest that what is most striking about these operations is that they closely resembled complex influence operations of the pre-AI age, but used AI to make some of the workflows easier. The journalist personas run by the Iranian operation bore a family resemblance to the fake journalist “Alice⁠(opens in a new window) Donovan⁠(opens in a new window),” a front for Russian military intelligence whose articles were published by a range of Western outlets in 2016-17. In 2020, individuals associated with past activity by the Russian Internet Research Agency ran a fake “news” outlet called “PeaceData⁠(opens in a new window),” which co-opted unwitting journalists around the world into writing for it.

These operations were also unusual for their potential reach. Using the IO Breakout Scale⁠(opens in a new window), which rates IO on a scale of 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest), we would assess the Russia-origin operation as belonging in Category 5. This is the first Category 5 operation we’ve disrupted since we began our reporting. The Iran-origin operation reached Category 4. Both managed to land their content (not all of which was generated from our models) in mainstream media outlets, rather than simply posting it on social media. This is consistent with a pattern we’ve observed across the 30 covert influence operations we’ve exposed in the last two and a half years: the operations which try to land their content in real media outlets, rather than relying on fake social media distribution, tend to have the highest potential reach and impact.

Sources indicate that matrix of the 30 IO we’ve exposed since early 2024, assessed by primary distribution method (social media, operation-run website, external publications) and score on the Breakout Scale. Operations which used more than one distribution method, such as running a website and promoting it on social media, are classified by the method which appeared to constitute the core of the operation.

AI can give such false-front operations greater scale, efficiency, linguistic fluency, and editorial ability. The operators can use these advantages to exploit unsuspecting victims, such as employees or editors, and plant their content in front of audiences who have no idea who was behind it, or what their motivations were. These operations also demonstrate the complexity and sophistication of threat actors’ use of false personas and entities to achieve their goals. Understanding the vulnerabilities that threat actors exploit in these efforts, and how those vulnerabilities can translate into audience and reach, will be essential to maintaining robust defenses across organizations.

But the covert nature of these false-front operations also makes them particularly vulnerable to responsible disclosure. Both “Alice Donovan” and “PeaceData” ceased their activity after they were exposed. That’s why our goal in reporting these false-front operations is to make further research and disruption easier—and make continuing the operations harder.

Russia-origin actors running influence campaigns across Latin America.

It has been revealed that we banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Russia. They used ChatGPT for a range of tasks associated with covert influence operations targeting countries across Latin America. Much of this activity appeared aimed at undermining Ukraine’s reputation in the region, but some appeared aimed at influencing local political outcomes, especially in Argentina and Bolivia. Most of the operators prompted in Russian; one prompted in Spanish, but nevertheless appeared to be located in Russia. We have shared information on this case with the relevant authorities.

The operators used ChatGPT to perform three main tasks: writing internal reports on their activities (and other people’s activities which they could plausibly take credit for), creating content for their operations, and drafting reports on the performance of a self-described “research platform” in Latin America called the Social Research Center (SRC). They appear to have controlled the SRC via a fake persona named “Mia Clark”; in honor of the name, we have nicknamed this operation “Dark Clark.” Since we do not allow access to our models from Russia, they used VPNs to connect to our services.

Sources indicate that in their internal reports, the operators claimed to have spread fake stories across Latin America to undermine Ukraine or local leaders. Some of these fakes have been attributed by open-source⁠(opens in a new window) researchers⁠(opens in a new window) to a Russian entity known as “Politology” or “La Compania,” a reported successor to the Wagner Group and other entities founded by Russian oligarch Yevgeniy Prigozhin. The operators also asked our models to translate or explain public reporting about Politology and Wagner, far more than asking about any other Russia-origin networks.

This operation was unusual in two ways. First, it appears to have successfully co-opted individuals in Latin America to work for the SRC. The Russian operators’ reports on the SRC referred to decisions over complications such as pay scales, hiring, and firing, suggesting that they controlled the entity, rather than cooperating with it. The available evidence indicates that the SRC’s employees in Latin America were not aware that they were working for a Russian group. Unlike another Russia-linked “think tank” that we recently exposed, the SRC appears to have produced a majority of original content via its co-opted staff. This stands out as the most complex attempt to run a front identity that we’ve disrupted over the past two and a half years.

Sources indicate that second, some open-source evidence suggests that Dark Clark’s fakes spread widely enough to provoke fact checks⁠(opens in a fresh window) and official denials⁠(opens in a new window), indicating a degree of penetration which goes beyond any of the influence operations we disrupted over the past two years. One fake that the operation claimed to have planted in Peru even fed into public tensions between Ukraine and Poland.

The main way the operators used ChatGPT was to draft and enhancement internal reports to an unknown superior. These regular reports described efforts to conduct covert influence campaigns across Latin America. They encompassed three main workstreams: efforts to denigrate Ukraine and undermine recruitment for the Ukrainian Armed Forces; efforts to interfere in the domestic politics of certain countries, especially Bolivia and Argentina; and management of the SRC. In the majority of cases, we did not observe the threat actors using our models to create content for the campaigns, only to report on them (the few exceptions are described below⁠).

The reports were rich in tactical detail, shining a light on how the operation sought to undermine Ukraine and some national leaders, notably the presidents of Argentina, Bolivia, and Ecuador. Some described efforts to trick locals into carrying out activities that the operators could weaponize; others described fake “leaks” that the operators claimed to have spread.

Industry observers note that in two cases, the evidence ties the operators to public reporting on “Politology.” The operators reported that, in 2024, they ran two campaigns targeting Argentina’s President Javier Milei. First, they said they spread a false report that Milei had bought Cartier jeweled collars for his dogs. Second, they claimed that they paid local actors to post anti-Milei graffiti in Buenos Aires. Based on leaked documents, both these claims have been publicly⁠(opens in a fresh window) attributed⁠(opens in a new window) to “Politology” and “La Compania.”.

Industry observers note that many more fakes have not been previously tied to Russian IO. For example, the operators claimed that in May 2026, they created a fake email address purporting to come from the Regional Directorate of Education in Lima, Peru. They used this to instruct schools in the district to hold events dedicated to Ukraine on the national Day of Cultural and Linguistic Diversity (May 21). The emails included explicit instructions to reference, among others, controversial twentieth-century Ukrainian nationalist Stepan Bandera, who is seen by some Ukrainians as an independence figure, but associated in Russia and Poland with fascism, wartime collaboration, and atrocities. According to the operators, some schools replied to the fake email address, confirming that they had held such events and even providing pictures.

The operators then claimed to have planted stories about the events in the media in both Peru and Poland, alongside allegations that Ukraine was “exporting” ultra-nationalist ideologies, triggering outrage. Open-source searches identified stories that matched this claim in the Peruvian⁠(opens in a fresh window) and⁠(opens in a new window) Polish⁠(opens in a new window) press⁠(opens in a new window), and an English-language publication in Hungary⁠(opens in a new window) (some of the articles have since been deleted). Some⁠(opens in a new window) articles⁠(opens in a new window) included a reaction from a Polish Member of the European Parliament proposing that people who indicated “anti-Polishness” be declared persona non grata in Poland. The Russian fake thus both fed on, and fed into, historical tensions between Ukrainians and Poles.

Similarly, in June, the operators claimed they used a different fake email address to trick schools in Ecuador into holding a ceremony pledging allegiance to President Daniel Noboa and to Erik Prince, former head of private military contractor Blackwater. The operators claimed that the incident provoked outrage in Ecuador and put pressure on the government to deny the fake, thus amplifying it to a nationwide audience. Again, open-source research identified media⁠(opens in a new window) coverage⁠(opens in a new window) in the Ecuadorian⁠(opens in a new window) press⁠(opens in a new window) that closely resembled this claim, and even a detailed rebuttal⁠(opens in a new window) by Ecuador’s Minister for Education.

The operators used a range of techniques to underpin their false stories. According to their internal reporting, they spread two different fakes targeting Ecuador in March. One used fake audio attributed to Ukraine’s consul in Ecuador, in which he was alleged to have made disparaging comments about Ecuadorians. Our open-source investigation identified a post on TikTok which matched this precise claim; it appeared to receive only limited engagement. The other described a fake video clip spread on X and TikTok under the logo of a genuine news channel, alleging that Noboa’s government was recruiting young men to fight in Ukraine. Fact checkers⁠(opens in a fresh window) in Ecuador described a campaign that matched this description in early April.

TikTok video posted on April 8, 2026, with the faked audio claimed by this operation and attributed to the Ukrainian Consul.

Sources indicate that another internal report described a fake they spread in Bolivia in late May, at the height of anti-government protests. The operators described the goal of this campaign explicitly as to exacerbate the crisis around the protests. The campaign featured a fake audio recording of a worker at the state water company, EPSAS, saying that the government was going to shut off water to the administrative capital, La Paz, and declare a state of emergency. Our open-source research identified a debunk⁠(opens in a latest window) of the matching claim and an official denial⁠(opens in a new window) from EPSAS.

According to recent reports, other internal reports included fakes that we were unable to corroborate from open sources, possibly because they had already been taken down, or failed to spread. For example, the operators claimed to have spread a story in January alleging that a Brazilian influencer and model had been trafficked into Ukraine by representatives of the Ukrainian Embassy, and had been killed in Kyiv. In June, they claimed to have spread another fake audio clip in Bolivia, this time purporting to come from an employee of the Central Bank of Bolivia, warning that the Bank was about to limit cash withdrawals. They also claimed to have spread a faked letter from the country’s hydrocarbons agency, warning of restrictions on fuel sales to private cars.

In a recent development, in other reports, the operators asked our models to help identify incidents in the target countries that they could take credit for, even if they had not been involved. For example, in Argentina, the operators claimed that the Argentinian Foreign Minister had quoted their operation in a United Nations committee meeting on the Falkland / Malvinas islands. The operators took credit for seeding the arguments that the principle of self-determination does not apply to the islands, and that the UK maintains a disproportionate military presence there. In fact, both arguments have been part of Argentina’s official position for many⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) years⁠(opens in a new window). Similarly, in June, Brazilian media reported⁠(opens in a new window) on the case of a Brazilian citizen who had travelled to Ukraine to join the army, been captured by Russian forces, and then made a televised statement claiming that he had been tricked into fighting. The ChatGPT operators tried to claim that this report reproduced their operation’s messaging; in fact, it quoted the captive’s own video⁠(opens in a new window). This suggests an attempt by the operators to run an influence operation targeting their own employers, rather than any external audience.

Some of the operators’ reports referred to a self-styled “research platform” called the Social Research Center (in Russian, Центр социологических исследований). According to the SRC’s website, it focuses on the Indian diaspora in Latin America, and relations between India and the countries of the region.

The internal reports suggested that the operators controlled the think tank, rather than merely working with it. They referenced, for example, hiring and firing decisions, pay scales, staffing intends, and ongoing research projects. Crucially, they also stated that the operators had created a fake persona, named “Mia Clark,” to run the operation’s social media activity and engage with staff on the ground in Latin America. The available evidence suggests that these on-the-ground employees had no idea that they were working for a Russian operation, and conducted research tasks in good faith. This use of unwitting cutouts strongly resembles the earlier Russian operation also linked to Prigozhin’s world, “PeaceData,” which Meta exposed⁠(opens in a latest window) in 2020.

Sources indicate that to judge by the Russian operators’ reports, their staff on the ground in Latin America conducted interviews with experts and commentators across the region, and then drafted research papers based on their findings. The topics ranged from a broad analysis of public opinion on the BRICS group, to a detailed comparison of the Brazilian economy under presidents Jair Bolsonaro and Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva. Sometimes, the Russian operators drafted status reports on the research projects before they had been published, indicating close engagement in the production process. We identified well over 60 articles on the SRC website, the great majority of which appeared to be original compositions. This sets Dark Clark apart from the Russia-origin operation we exposed recently, which also ran a think tank as a front, but plagiarized most of its content; it suggests an intention to build a more durable front entity, with contacts throughout Latin America.

Sources indicate that to promote the SRC’s work, the Russian operators claimed that they had tried to create a network of social media assets. According to their reports, this social media activity ran into problems when operators in different parts of the world tried to access the same accounts, leading to account restrictions. Traces of this can be seen in the open-source record: for example, the transparency settings of the main SRC account on X showed a German location (possibly as a result of VPN use) but a connection via the Russian Federation App Store, while the transparency settings of one of its Instagram accounts showed an admin location in Venezuela. None of the three SRC-branded Facebook accounts that we identified had enough followers to trigger admin location settings.

In a recent development, left, X account linked to the Social Research Center. Note the transparency setting that shows the account connected via the Russian Federation app store. Right, SRC Instagram account: note the Venezuela location.

Sources indicate that the operators reported particular problems on LinkedIn, where they mentioned they created an explicitly fake account to represent SRC, but then struggled to build a network for it. According to their reports, the solution was to create more fake accounts to follow the first one and make it look more convincing. As of August 17, a LinkedIn account with the same Social Research Center branding counted 961 followers and claimed 200-500 staff, but only listed two employees.

Sources indicate that occasionally, as well as using AI to patch reports, the operators did ask our model to help design and create texts that they could use in their operations: for example, asking for help in making sure that their fakes used the correct accent, vocabulary, and institutional style for different countries. This was a relatively small proportion of the overall workload, perhaps because the operation appears to have included at least one native Spanish speaker from Latin America, and therefore had less need of AI language support.

Sources indicate that for example, on one occasion, one of the Russian-speaking operators asked the model to help draft, in Russian, a letter which would implicate Ukraine’s honorary consul to Panama in corruption. The Spanish-speaking operator then asked the model to translate the letter into Spanish, and to generate an audio script to accompany it. A photo that matched the text of the letter, with a voiceover that matched the operator’s script, was posted on TikTok by an account that purported to be a news outlet, but with the logo of Panama’s TVN Noticias⁠(opens in a newly introduced window). The TikTok channel only had one follower, and stopped posting after it planted this fake.

TikTok post showing the letter whose text was generated by this operation, with a voiceover script likewise generated by the operation.

On another occasion, the Spanish-speaking operator in Russia gave the model a Russian-language script that claimed Noboa had insulted poor people in Ecuador, and asked the model to translate it into Ecuadorian Spanish. On a third, in March, the same user asked the model to proofread a draft Spanish-language contract between a manufacturer called “International Security Solutions FZE” and an individual in Ecuador, purporting to provide infrastructure services in Ukraine. The user’s questions focused on how to improve the language and layout, including asking which words should be in bold.

According to recent reports, the user’s prompts about the contract finished once the wording was finalized. Open-source research, however, shows that a picture of the “contract” was subsequently circulated on social media⁠(opens in a new window). It was used to bolster the claim that Noboa’s government had worked with a front firm to trick Ecuadorians into being recruited into the Ukrainian army. The fake spread widely enough to trigger a fact check⁠(opens in a new window) in early April: the fact checkers concluded that the company “does not appear in the registry of Ecuador’s Superintendency of Companies, Securities, and Insurance”.

The impact of this operation requires particularly careful assessment. As noted above, one of the operators’ main approaches was to take credit for activity which had nothing to do with their operation. As such, their own claims of impact in their internal reporting cannot be taken at face value. Similarly, some of the fake stories that they claimed to have planted did not show up in open-source research, potentially because they were spread in non-public channels, already taken down, or not actually posted.

However, open-source evidence allowed us to corroborate some of the claims that they made. Some of the fakes that the operation claimed to have spread were subsequently reported by fact checkers and debunked by governments, suggesting that they had spread widely enough to merit a response. In other cases, we were able to identify content online that closely matched the content generated by this operation. Most notably, the operation’s claim to have tricked a Peruvian school into holding an event that portrayed Bandera was subsequently reported on in both Latin America and Europe, and appears to have led to comment from at least one Polish MEP.

Using the IO Breakout Scale⁠(opens in a fresh window), which rates IO on a scale of 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest), we would assess this operation as belonging in Category 5, with evidence that suggests that it led to public comment by politicians in a number of countries. This is the first Category 5 operation we’ve disrupted since we began our reporting.

Iran-origin operation seeding long-form articles under deceptive bylines in online news outlets.

According to recent reports, we banned a cluster of ChatGPT accounts that originated in Iran. They prompted in Persian, and generated content in Persian and English. The actors obscured their location by using VPNs to access ChatGPT.

Industry observers note that the operation used our models to refine long-form articles and editorial pitches, generate social media comments, and refine internal reports. The operators used seven different bylines to pitch their articles, so we have dubbed their campaign “Bogus Bylines.” The long-form articles focused on the US-Iran conflict. The majority of the comments likewise dealt with the conflict; a minority dealt with US politics, typically in the wider context of the conflict.

The apparent impact of their main workstreams varied significantly. We identified almost 100 articles published or syndicated under the operation’s bylines across roughly a dozen online outlets around the world. These were small to medium outlets, generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East. By contrast, none of the social media comments appears to have generated substantial engagement in terms of likes, shares, or further replies. In fact, the operators’ internal reports used a deceptive calculation to measure their social media impact, possibly in an attempt to inflate the operators’ apparent effectiveness.

The overall activity appeared consistent with a commercial actor running a for-hire influence campaign, but we are unable to identify the particular actor involved. We have shared information on this case with the relevant authorities.

This operation’s most far-reaching activity consisted of asking ChatGPT to review and refine long-form, English-language articles about the geopolitics of the US-Iran conflict. Typical prompts asked the model to assess an English-language draft against the submission criteria for a specific online outlet, and suggest edits to make sure it complied. Once the operators approved the edits, they asked the model to generate an email that they could use to pitch the article to the editor of the online outlet in question.

Recent findings suggest that these pitching messages were drafted using seven different fake bylines: Ervin B. Hoskins, Noah Lamington, Sophia Gonzalez, Michael Harrison, Ericka Feusier, Jenny Williams, and Alice Johnson. According to the biographies that were posted online alongside some of these articles, each persona purported to be a Western journalist (usually American, though the Noah Lamington persona’s bio claimed that they were in Latest Zealand), often with a focus on international politics, the Middle East, human rights, or conflict. For one of the personas, “Michael Harrison,” the operators asked the model to write the bio itself. (Of note, in March Meta disrupted⁠(opens in a new window) an Iranian IO that also featured a “Michael Harrison” journalist persona.).

According to recent reports, some of these personas were backstopped by accounts across a range of social media platforms. The Michael Harrison persona, for example, was backstopped on Medium, X, and Facebook. The Ervin B. Hoskins persona featured accounts on X, Facebook, Instagram, and Threads. This persona’s bio claimed to be “an American freelance writer”, but social media transparency settings located the accounts in Iran.

According to recent reports, top, Instagram bio for the Ervin Hoskins persona. Bottom left, X account transparency information, showing the use of the West Asia Android app. Bottom right, Instagram account transparency information, showing location in Iran. Meta banned the Instagram account in August.

Using open-source investigation techniques, we identified almost 100 articles that had been published under one or other of the operators’ bylines, across over a dozen different publications. These publications generally focused on international affairs, geopolitics, and events in the Middle East, sometimes from an antiwar or progressive point of view. The earliest article we identified was published in July 2025, and the latest in October 2026. The frequency of articles greatly increased after the outbreak of the US-Iran conflict.

In a recent development, timeline of articles, by author and theme, July 2025—September 2026. Note the density of publications on US-Iran relations from March 2026 onwards.

Sample headlines of articles published under the bylines linked to this operation between February and July 2026 in a range of online outlets.

At least some of the articles were then promoted by the social media accounts of the outlets in question, giving the Iranian operators a potential way to access audiences that they would not otherwise have reached.

Alongside the articles, the threat actors asked ChatGPT to generate batches of comments on geopolitical or political topics in English or Persian. The actors’ typical approach was to input the text or a screenshot of a social media post, and ask the model for a set of replies that aligned with their overall focus. These were then posted online, often within a few minutes of each other. The operators’ internal reporting referred to both human and automated posting; we have no evidence to suggest that this automation was carried out with the help of our models.

Tweets in English, left, and Persian, right, generated by this operation and posted in July. The English-language comments replied to an English-language tweet warning that the US was preparing a “large scale assault” on Iran. All the comments in this image were posted in a 10-minute span. The Persian-language comments replied to a Persian-language tweet about US strikes on Iran, and were posted within 13 minutes.

Industry observers note that some of this batch commenting activity consisted of generating replies to social media posts about the operation’s own news articles. Here, the operators input screenshots of posts that promoted their articles, and then generated comments that praised or endorsed them, likely to make the articles look more popular.

Facebook post by a local US news Page sharing an article generated by the operation, and comments on that post generated by the operation.

Sources indicate that the majority of the comment batches focused more generally on the conflict between Iran, the United States, and Israel. The customers asked for comments on topics such as missile strikes, ceasefires, and diplomatic maneuvering, specifying outputs that portrayed the US as the aggressor, Israel as an unreliable ally of the US, and Iran as a defiant but resilient victim. The operators generated a particularly large number of replies to posts by UK-based satellite network Iran International—a critic of the Iranian regime—generating over two dozen batches of hostile Persian-language replies. A minority of the batches generated replies to social media posts about US political complications, typically also in the wider context of the conflict.

Instagram comments generated by this operation in reply to posts about US politics.

It has been revealed that we identified a small number of these replies being posted online; many more did not appear in our open-source searches, potentially because they were either not posted, or posted by accounts that had already been taken down. (For example, three of the journalist personas—Ericka Feusier, Alice Johnson, and Jenny Williams—listed X account handles in their published bios: all had been suspended as of August 2026.) Some of the accounts that did post comments online had Western-seeming names, but showed account locations in Iran.

The transparency settings of the Instagram accounts that made the comments illustrated above, showing that they were located in Iran.

Industry observers note that where we did find these replies being posted, they typically made up a minority of total comments on the post in question, suggesting that the operators were not a dominant voice among the authentic responses. Nor did they appear to have attracted substantial engagement: indeed, many of the likes on the operation’s replies came from accounts that were themselves linked to the operation. We have shared information on this case with industry partners, who are best placed to provide holistic assessments on engagement.

It has been revealed that the attempt to make their activity look more popular was not limited to public-facing posts. Alongside their content generation, the operators occasionally asked ChatGPT to refine what appeared to be internal reports about their social media campaign. This typically consisted of providing the model with a series of statistics, and asking it to turn them into polished presentations.

Industry observers note that this is not the first operation we’ve disrupted that used AI to write its own⁠(opens in a upcoming window) self-review⁠(opens in a new window). What was most striking about the Iranian operators’ efforts to mark their own homework was the method they used to do so. The main “impact” metric they used was the number of views on the posts to which they replied (not the number of views on the actual replies), counted before, and an unspecified amount of time after, the replies were posted. This calculation did not account for any views which may have been the result of other factors, such as the original posts’ popularity or other comments. As such, it greatly exaggerated the operation’s impact figures, suggesting that the operators either did not know a more effective way of calculating them, or did not choose to use it.

In fact, based on the evidence that can be gleaned from open-source observation, the operation’s two main workstreams appear to have had very different degrees of likely impact.

In a recent development, the social media replies that we were able to identify generally enjoyed low numbers of likes, views, and comments (in the single or double digits). As noted above, the replies typically made up a minority of total comments on the post in question. Using the IO Breakout Scale⁠(opens in a fresh window), which rates IO on a scale of 1 (lowest) to 6 (highest), we would assess this part of the operation at Category 2, with comments on multiple platforms, but little sign of breakout or ability to dominate the replies.

By contrast, the journalist personas succeeded in getting their articles published by a range of outlets, some with substantial followings: for example, one of the online outlets that published this operation’s articles had almost 2 million followers on Facebook, almost 355,000 followers on X, and over 544,000 on Instagram as of August 2026. We would assess this part of the operation as a Category 4, based on its consistent breakout to a number of media outlets.

LegalOn halves Codex costs while maintaining development speed
