📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.
  • Sources indicate that legalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions.
  • Recent findings suggest that this approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

LegalOn cut costs by 65% while maintaining development speed by matching Astra, Sol, and Luna to tasks and managing budgets strategically.

Cost reduction in mature business areas.

Reduction in estimated daily costs.

Sources indicate that legalOn Technologies offers Professional AI globally, using AI to support legal work and other key business functions. By combining domain expertise with AI, it enables people to focus on complex judgments and decisions. Its goal is AI-driven management that improves the quality and speed of business decision-making.

Recent findings suggest that this approach extends beyond its products to making the organization itself AI-native. The organization integrated Codex into its development process and expanded adoption across the organization through day-to-day use.

Industry observers note that as adoption took hold, a fresh challenge emerged: cost control. Unlimited use of high-performance models could drive up spending, while blanket restrictions risked undermining the productivity gains AI had enabled.

Recent findings suggest that how could it reduce costs without slowing development? LegalOn Technologies addressed this challenge by selecting among GPT‑6 (Astra, Luna) and GPT‑6.1 Sol based on task complexity and development stage, and aligning budgets with each business’s stage of growth. The company halved costs while maintaining development speed.

The tech giant initially gave developers unlimited access to its main model, GPT‑5.5 in Fast mode. They expanded its use to design, implementation, and everyday work, learning through experimentation how best to divide responsibilities between people and AI.

Industry observers note that continuing to use high-performance models without limits, however, would inevitably exceed the annual budget. The company's AI-powered Development CoE (AID CoE) began developing guidelines for model selection. AID CoE tested and monitored models, while managers shared its findings with their teams. This enabled each engineer to independently choose the most suitable model for each task.

According to recent reports, the newly introduced guidelines shifted the tech giant from using the highest-capability model for every task to choosing the right model for the job. Teams started with a lightweight model and moved to more capable models as task complexity increased.

To support governance, the company also introduced system controls through administrator settings, with monthly usage limits for departments and individuals. AID CoE monitors usage and adjusts limits as business needs require.

Internal testing under these controls helped make the selection criteria more specific. GPT‑6 Luna, the lightest model, handles code implementation with clear requirements; GPT‑6.1 Sol supports standard design, data analysis, and document preparation; and GPT‑6 Astra, the most capable model, handles advanced judgment, including architecture design. Matching models to tasks gradually became a shared practice across teams.

Everyday execution and implementation; running everyday automations; delegating relatively simple tasks and analysis; code implementation, mainly as a subagent.

Standard design and analysis; relatively simple software design; routine numerical analysis and document creation; tasks requiring shorter completion times than with Luna.

Complex analysis, design, and orchestration; complex analysis and document creation; complex software design; coordinating agents as the orchestrator.

Alongside model selection, the firm began restricting Fast mode by default, allowing individual requests only when needed. Although the change raised concerns about development speed, teams used approaches such as running tasks in parallel to maintain performance and transition smoothly.

It also introduced budget caps for AI spending at the department, group, and individual levels. The established LegalOn business was asked to improve cost efficiency by up to approximately 20%, while new businesses in the launch phase received generous budgets to encourage active use of AI.

According to recent reports, yuta Tokitake, Senior Engineering Manager at LegalOn Technologies, explains that new businesses prioritized business speed over cost efficiency. The aim was to use AI extensively to increase output and ultimately drive business growth.

Sources indicate that together, model selection, feature restrictions, and budgets tailored to each business reduced estimated daily costs by approximately 65%. This approach kept the overall budget under control while directing resources toward businesses the firm wanted to grow.

Model optimization and strategic resource allocation delivered the following results:.

A shift from using the most capable model for every task to selecting GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6.1 Sol, or GPT‑6 Luna based on task complexity and development stage.

Development performance maintained after restricting Fast mode by default, supported by team practices such as parallel task execution.

Budget caps that combined approximately 20% greater efficiency in mature businesses with active investment in new businesses.

A 65% reduction in estimated daily costs compared with GPT‑5.5 by choosing among GPT‑6 and 6.1 models.

Through model optimization, the manufacturer reduced costs without sacrificing development speed or quality. Teams are also seeing AI steadily shorten the cycle from development to release.

Recent findings suggest that but the organization is looking further ahead. Does faster development alone make AI investment a success? The connection between faster development and customer value remained unclear. “It is almost a given that AI can accelerate system development and updates,” states Tokitake. “What we really want to understand is whether that faster development actually translates into value for customers.”.

This question prompted the company to develop its own metric, shifting the basis for evaluating AI investment from development speed and usage volume to customer value.

Tokitake explains: “When using AI, we can track the cost of individual tasks, but the total cost of a complete piece of work—a feature release—often remains a black box. So we designed the measurement around each feature release as a single unit. By linking the customer value that release delivers to the actual AI costs invested in it, we aim to make the return on investment visible and accurate.”.

The organization is right now building the pipeline to calculate this metric. Once complete, it will make the true ROI in terms of customer value visible. LegalOn Technologies is moving beyond AI cost management toward directly connecting technology investment with business value.

The next goal is to turn individual engineers' AI know-how into an organization-wide capability. As a first step, the company looks to build a knowledge base to collect and share practical experience. It will capture knowledge such as the best model combinations for design, implementation, and review, and quickly turn individual successes into company-wide best practices.

Recent findings suggest that these changes, driven by teams' practical experience, are also shaping the organization and hiring. AI-driven productivity gains are prompting the tech giant to fundamentally rethink how work is divided between people and AI, as well as its workforce intends. It has already begun emphasizing AI skills in hiring, as its investment strategy and organizational structure evolve.

In a recent development, turning AI adoption into a lasting competitive advantage requires continually refining the balance between governance and teams' freedom to act. AID CoE and the security team are working together to optimize performance, cost, and risk from multiple perspectives, building a flexible framework that supports experimentation across the organization.

Pollo AI turns creative ideas into campaigns with OpenAI

💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.
  • Pollo AI⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise.
  • “We want to do for video what Canva did for design.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GPT‑5.6, GPT‑6 Astra, and GPT‑Image‑2.5, Pollo AI helps creators turn bold ideas into detailed images and cinematic video ads.

Pollo AI⁠(opens in a newly introduced window) was founded on the premise that people should be able to turn their creative ideas into finished images and videos without needing production expertise. Even with generative AI, creators and marketers can struggle to navigate different tools and choose between models to get the result they want. Some may even abandon their projects in frustration.

“We want to do for video what Canva did for design. We want to make it easy enough that more people can actually use it, not just the ones who already know how,” explains Bill Zhu, the founder and CEO of Pollo AI. Today, Pollo AI serves more than 26 million customers who use the platform to create videos, ads, and visual content.

The team’s first breakthrough was video templates. Now, 30% of creator sessions start from these templates or trending-format workflows. Building on this success, the firm’s latest offering is Pollo Agent. It uses OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, to provide a fully guided workflow for video creation, including this post-apocalyptic adventure from a Pollo AI user.

Pollo Agent interprets the user’s rough ideas and visual references, and then develops storylines, scene flows, and scripts. CTO Peter Zhou says OpenAI models stood out for their ability to understand ambiguous creative inputs and their multimodal capability, sharing: “GPT‑5.6 performed especially well there.” The team also remarked they value the OpenAI API’s stability and release cadence.

Sources indicate that to balance reasoning depth, speed, and cost, Pollo AI uses GPT‑5.6 for routing and GPT‑6 Astra for more challenging work, such as developing a narrative or planning scene revisions. This model mix lets the system match the level of reasoning to the task based on the user’s prompt. Pollo AI reports that users spend more than 50% less time choosing or switching models, giving them more time for creativity.

Pollo AI tests generative models against real user prompts and workflows, evaluating output quality, consistency, stylistic range, speed, and cost. GPT‑Image‑2.5 was selected to handle image generation, helping creators make posters, storyboards, and campaign visuals.

Pollo AI’s primary people are content creators, and the platform is especially popular for creating micro dramas with both AI and human actors. However, more marketers and business owners are starting to use Pollo AI to develop video content swiftly and easily too.

Industry observers note that pollo’s Photo to Video Ads tool in its Marketing Studio suite uses OpenAI models to turn a still image and prompt into a short video. It’s designed to help small businesses and DTC brands generate product ads for social media in minutes rather than days.

In a recent development, one Pollo AI user wanted to use a product photo to make a fragrance ad that felt luxurious. The static photo alone could not convey that mood, and a professional video shoot was beyond their budget.

Using Photo to Video Ad, the user turned their starting image into a roughly 15-second video ad. The tool generated velvet textures, warm spotlights, and close-ups of the bottle to establish the mood across the sequence and ended it with the fragrance framed against deep red fabric.

Another customer, a jewelry brand, wanted a bold editorial campaign image, but its budget could not stretch to a high-concept studio shoot.

Using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, the brand was able to turn its creative vision of its statement jewelry on a model seated beside a cheetah into reality. The tool framed the scene with dark drapery and warm lighting and ensured that the brand’s jewelry products were highly visible.

The customer got a finished luxury campaign visual with lower production effort, time, and cost compared to live shoot.

Pollo AI also makes it easy for customers to start with a product photo and leverage OpenAI models to turn it into an image that’s far more creative. For example, a beverage brand wanted its peach soda to feel playful and imaginative in an advertising campaign, but a standard studio product shot could not capture what the team had in mind.

Sources indicate that using Pollo Agent and GPT‑Image‑2.5, which brings sharper details and faster generation to creative workflows, the team transformed a simple bottle image into a snowy miniature landscape, complete with a train, lizards, and sparkling droplets. The finished image created a playful scene the brand could use in its campaign.

Pollo wants AI video to become part of everyday content creation over the next 12 months. For Zhu, that depends on making it even easier to turn an idea into an asset ready to post, test, or use in a campaign, something Pollo AI is enabled to deliver with the continued improvement of OpenAI models and image generation.

“We think the AI shift in content creation will favor products that make creation more repeatable from the start, with stronger formats, less trial and error, and a simpler workflow around the models themselves,” he claims.

💡 Key Takeaways
  • Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.
  • Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.
  • Over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Across recruiting, engineering, and operations, Oracle turns specialist knowledge into fast, repeatable workflows with ChatGPT Work and Codex.

Decrease in the time it takes for talent acquisition research.

Over a hundred thousand employees across Oracle are using ChatGPT Work and Codex, from talent acquisition to Oracle Applications Lab to the IT organization. In each case, work that used to rely on specialists and take days can now be done by anyone and is complete in minutes. Recruiters skip days of market research, business users describe an outcome instead of hunting for a report, and technical leads build tools that used to take a full team months.

In a recent development, the talent acquisition team used ChatGPT Work to build a talent market intelligence tool that takes a job description, researches comparable roles, benchmarks compensation, and assesses the talent pool across relevant locations. The tool arms the recruiter with valuable information that they need going into a conversation with the hiring manager, information that previously took 2–4 days to compile.

Sources indicate that “We’ve gone from zero to a hundred,” notes Jan Ackerman, Senior Vice President and Global Head of Talent Acquisition at Oracle. “Now we’re able to sit down and prep for about 15 to 20 minutes using the tool that we’ve built using [ChatGPT] Work.”.

Industry observers note that not only is the process faster, but it’s also more consistent. Recruiters used to run the intake process differently from one search to the next, but with the talent market intelligence tool, the process is consistent, so every hiring manager has the same quality of data and insights, no matter which recruiter they worked with.

Sources indicate that the Oracle Applications Lab team, which helps run many of Oracle’s core business processes, built an ontology of the manufacturer’s objects, relationships, and rules, so a plain-language business question can be turned into a reliable SQL query with Codex. A business user describes the outcome they want, and Codex decides which internal systems to call, gathers the information, and returns an analysis, a report, or an application.

That’s a change from how work used to get done. Lam stated one user came to him after asking a question that would normally have taken her a couple of hours to answer. She told Lam, “With the fresh tool, I put in the request and got a response almost immediately.” When she checked the result against the old manual process, the numbers matched exactly.

Recent findings suggest that in production engineering, site reliability engineers use Codex to gather relevant context about an incident and automatically pull up the right playbook. SREs spend more time guiding decisions and less time hunting for information. “A typical simple incident that used to take an hour to resolve can now be handled in minutes,” says Lam.

Even as Codex takes on more of the work, Lam is careful to note that none of this runs on autopilot. Someone still has to make sure the underlying system is built right.

While AI builds the tools, the people are still responsible for the output. A few lessons stand out:.

Recent findings suggest that give the correct guardrails. “You have to still be very responsible about your system design, your architecture, your security, and how you would like Codex to structure the code for you,” indicates Lam.

Provide prototypes instead of specs. “Normally, I put [my idea] down on paper, but now I put it down in a prototype,” states Barry Shilmover, Vice President and Technical Advisor to the CIO.

It has been revealed that own the code. “If you don’t work alongside Codex, you’re going to get into a situation of having lots of code that is not going to be maintainable,” says Lam.

In a recent development, the Oracle team is completely shifting how the company operates with AI. Across recruiting, analytics, and engineering, each line of business described an outcome and let Codex and ChatGPT handle how the work gets done. With thousands of ChatGPT and Codex owners already, Oracle employees use AI across countless work tasks. As Shilmover puts it, “I don’t know what the answer is because I don’t know what my next problem to solve will be. I just know that one of the first things I’ll do is I’ll leverage Codex to do that.”.

Asana cuts model costs 76x in browser tests with GPT-6.1 Sol

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 6 min read (1123 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~6 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.
  • Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
  • Faster browser runs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex, Asana made its browser agent 76x cheaper and 5x faster in tests to offer customers more capable models.

Lower estimated model costs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

Faster browser runs with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

Average estimated model cost with the optimized GPT-6.1 Sol workflow.

With GPT‑6 Astra in Codex running experiments, Asana optimized its browser agent’s workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol to run 76x cheaper and 5x faster.

Asana helps customers automate work across business applications through StackAI⁠(opens in a latest window), a platform it acquired⁠(opens in a new window). Using StackAI, customers can build workflows that navigate websites, fill out forms, and gather information without writing code. At Asana’s scale, small inefficiencies in these workflows add up.

In a recent development, asana’s StackAI CTO, Frank Hidalgo, PhD, set out to make the browser agent faster and cheaper to run. He directed GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to investigate the agent, test improvements, and compare the results. Work he estimates would have taken one to two months by hand took about a week.

Asana’s 144-run study⁠(opens in a new window) tested GPT‑6.1 Sol and three other frontier models, called here Models A, B and C. The optimized workflow that emerged on GPT‑6.1 Sol averaged $0.47 in estimated model costs and about four minutes per run, 76x cheaper and 5x faster than the original production setup on Model B.

To move swiftly, Hidalgo started by using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to map the codebase and explain how the agent built each model request. GPT‑6 Astra discovered that the agent cached its fixed instructions and tool definitions, but not the growing history of page text and screenshots it gathered, so every request resent that history at full price.

The agent also dropped older screenshots and trimmed text at nearly every step. Each edit altered the history, so caching the history alone would not have helped, and losing those facts could require the agent to revisit pages it had already read.

Hidalgo reviewed GPT‑6 Astra’s proposed fixes and selected three to test:.

Extending caching to the agent’s browsing history.

Increasing the amount of text it could retain.

Removing screenshots in batches rather than at every step.

It has been revealed that GPT‑6 Astra began with quick tests to establish which variables mattered. Because the code was not designed for controlled experiments, it then refactored the code so one frontend and backend could support many workflows in parallel, each with its own settings.

Astra conducted the full study: history budgets of 120,000 and 480,000 characters and six caching and screenshot policies, each tested three times on each of the four models (see the table below). The best-performing policy allowed screenshots to accumulate to 20 before cutting back to the most recent one. This kept earlier history unchanged for longer stretches between removals. Combined with the larger history budget, it became the optimized workflow. Each configuration performed the same task: collecting six fields for each of 32 books from a public demo catalog, representative of what some Asana customers run in StackAI.

A smaller, less expensive model from another frontier lab, released Fall 2025.

The model originally used in production, from the same lab as Model A, released Summer 2026.

An updated version of Model B, released Fall 2026.

Recent findings suggest that GPT‑6 Astra ran the workflows and examined the requests, usage records and outputs, and separate model sessions reviewed the work. Every session’s requests, data traces and results were recorded in Command⁠(opens in a fresh window), Asana’s software delivery platform, so the team could review the complete study afterward. From Command, the findings were turned into tickets, then pull requests, and the changes went to production.

Recent findings suggest that for Model B, the optimization reduced estimated model cost from at least $36.21 (some original runs reached the step limit before they finished) to $1.24 per run, a reduction of 29x. The optimized workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol was 2.6x cheaper still, at $0.47. Every run in the optimized workflow completed the task and returned the correct answer.

Means of 3 runs. ≥: the baseline includes capped runs, so its mean is a lower bound.

The two right folds compare against Model B optimized. Model B ran in phase 1, Model C and Sol 6.1 in phase 2 of the same study (dotted line).

On GPT‑6.1 Sol alone, with the larger history budget, the upcoming caching and screenshot policy reduced cost 4x, from $1.97 to $0.47 per run. Each call was about 3x cheaper, because 89% of the input came from cache at 5% of the uncached price. Runs also became faster: at least 22.5 minutes on the original setup on Model B, roughly four minutes with the optimized workflow on GPT‑6.1 Sol.

Mean of 3 runs, SD whiskers. ≥: mean includes a capped or unfinished run, so the true value is at least this large.

According to recent reports, bars use the blue theme. Read caching effects against the 480k larger-budget bar.

Run markers and SD whiskers are approximate reconstructions from the source image; underlying run values and standard deviations were not available.

Mean of 3 runs, SD whiskers. ≥: mean includes a capped or unfinished run, so the true value is at least this large.

It has been revealed that bars use the blue theme. Read caching effects against the 480k larger-budget bar.

Run markers and SD whiskers are approximate reconstructions from the source image; underlying run values and standard deviations were not available.

Recent findings suggest that the investigation also demonstrated how history management affected whether the agent produced an answer at all. Giving GPT‑6.1 Sol more room to retain its browsing history increased the number of runs that produced an answer from three of 18 with the smaller history budget to all 18 with the larger budget, each with the correct answer. For Hidalgo, the business value is giving customers access to faster, more capable models while keeping operating costs sustainable.

Recent findings suggest that asana has released the changes to browser navigation in StackAI and is developing tools to make similar experiments easier to repeat. Over time, the team prepares to incorporate this testing into the platform’s evaluations, so customers and internal teams can compare cost, runtime, and answer quality when configuring their agents.

Asana is now using GPT‑6 Astra in Codex to test product features before release: Astra navigates the platform, tries different inputs and reports bugs for human QA reviewers. Hidalgo views this as the foundation for a new software development lifecycle, with many cloud agent sessions testing features in parallel.

The complete study is available on the Asana⁠(opens in a fresh window) and StackAI⁠(opens in a new window) blogs.

Sophos cuts threat investigation time by 96% with OpenAI Daybreak

📅 09 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 4 min read (773 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~4 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos combines frontier intelligence with cybersecurity expertise to investigate threats faster and protect customers at scale.
  • reduction in investigation time using OpenAI models.
  • Sources indicate that frontier AI is changing cybersecurity on both sides⁠(opens in a new window).
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos combines frontier intelligence with cybersecurity expertise to investigate threats faster and protect customers at scale.

average response time for cases using AI agents.

reduction in investigation time using OpenAI models.

of MDR cases resolved end-to-end by AI.

Sources indicate that frontier AI is changing cybersecurity on both sides⁠(opens in a new window). Advanced models can help defenders find and investigate threats faster. But those capabilities are also spreading to open-weight models, giving attackers new ways to discover vulnerabilities and accelerate exploitation.

Sophos⁠(opens in a new window) is one of the companies standing in their way, protecting more than 625,000 organisations across sectors and regions. “We see a huge variety of different attacks,” notes John Peterson, the company’s Chief Technology Officer. “We’ve cultivated vast expertise in combating them over four decades in the cybersecurity business.”.

Through OpenAI Daybreak, Sophos is combining OpenAI models with its own threat intelligence, response playbooks and security expertise. The aim isn’t simply to give analysts another tool. It’s to increase the impact of Sophos’s expertise across every customer it protects.

“Sophos brings the domain expertise and the know-how to combat attacks at scale. Programmes like Daybreak, and companies like OpenAI, bring frontier intelligence that allows us to take that domain expertise and scale it to support all of our customers.”.

At the centre of the work is Sophos Fusion, the Sophos AI-native cyber defense system that includes Sophos Managed Detection and Response (MDR). It brings together sensor data from more than 500 third-party integrations alongside Sophos’s own products. Together, those sensors generate trillions of events every day, which Sophos distills into roughly 1,000 to 2,000 cases for its nine security operations centres to investigate.

Agents built through Daybreak have changed how those cases are handled. An investigation agent gathers the customer context, detections, indicators of compromise (IoCs) and relevant threat intelligence for each case. A planning model then creates a proposal–execute–review loop: building an investigation plan, completing the steps and producing a summary with recommended response actions for analysts to review. Other agents can carry out parts of the response.

Sources indicate that before Daybreak, investigating and responding to a case depended primarily on human expertise. Sophos’s existing process averaged around 38 minutes — performance Peterson says was better than 96% of professional security operations centres.

“Now, because of the agents we’ve been able to build through the Daybreak programme, the average response time for cases using those agents has fallen to about 89 seconds. About half of the cases we handle are now being automated by agents we developed using the Daybreak models.”.

Sophos has built customer control into its MDR service through three operating modes:.

Notify: Sophos investigates the case and recommends a response, but the customer acts.

Collaborate: Sophos and the customer work together before action is taken.

Authorise: Sophos can respond directly on the customer’s behalf.

The same boundaries apply whether work is completed by a person or an agent. Sophos uses automation to move quickly and make better use of analysts’ time, but potentially destructive actions still require the right level of human oversight.

“Anything we don’t feel comfortable with an agent handling gets passed off for human judgement,” Peterson confirms.

Reduced the average response time for cases using agents from approximately 38 minutes to 89 seconds.

Enabled Sophos to resolve 52% of MDR cases end-to-end with AI, within boundaries calibrated by Sophos analysts.

Gives customers a faster and more consistent investigation experience.

Helps Sophos scale compute rather than relying on equivalent growth in scarce cybersecurity headcount.

Returns analysts’ attention to the threats, exceptions and decisions where their expertise matters most.

Peterson says Sophos will keep expanding what its agents can do. “The response capabilities are going to continue to become more sophisticated, and we’re going to broaden the range of use cases we address with the agents we’ve built.”.

“With programmes like Daybreak, we have an opportunity to stay a step ahead of the attacker community.”.

According to recent reports, his advice for other security leaders is simple: “The one thing security leaders should do tomorrow is really come back to focusing on the security fundamentals for their organization,” he claims. “That of course includes patching. But patches are only ever going to include vulnerabilities that are known by the vendor.”.

The answer is to maintain “a layered security approach” that includes endpoint protection, multifactor authentication (MFA), network segmentation and strong security operations. “Vulnerabilities are being discovered at an alarming rate and exploited at a scale that we’ve never seen. So I think doing the fundamentals well is more important today than it’s ever been.”.

  • It has been revealed that longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Higgsfield brings creators longer videos with GPT‑6 Astra, precise visuals with GPT‑Image‑2.5, and a path to voice filmmaking with GPT‑Live.

Higgsfield AI⁠(opens in a upcoming window) is on a mission to make professional video and image creation accessible to anyone with an idea. Before GPT‑6 Astra, those videos topped out at around one minute. Now, says CEO and co-founder Alex Mashrabov, owners can create videos over 10 minutes long.

It has been revealed that longer videos are just one way Higgsfield AI helps smaller creative teams take on more ambitious work. According to Alex, with models like GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑Image‑2.5, it’s now possible for a single creator to execute high-end fashion campaigns from start to finish.

Higgsfield AI’s creative agents take on repetitive production tasks, such as creating multiple variations of a shot. With GPT‑6 Astra, those agents can also call external tools to handle complex, manual work in 3D modeling. Alex indicates that capability helps address one of creative AI’s hardest problems: maintaining consistency across longer videos.

Being able to create longer instructional videos also matters to Alex personally. He supports rural schools in Kazakhstan and describes an early effort using GPT‑6 Astra’s visual understanding to identify topics students may be struggling with and create videos tailored to what they need to learn.

It has been revealed that for small businesses creating promotional content, having readable text and precise infographics can be just as crucial as the image itself. GPT‑Image‑2.5 makes that kind of content possible for businesses without large production budgets, Alex indicates.

“GPT‑Image‑2.5 is state of the art and the first model of its kind that can reliably render the text and infographics on top of the imagery,” he says.

Industry observers note that higgsfield AI builds its product through close collaboration between around 200 creatives and 100 engineers. Codex gives the creative team “the power of a really strong software engineer,” shares Alex.

Creatives use Codex to turn their ideas into software prototypes. Previously, bringing those prototypes into production required heavy involvement from front-end and back-end engineers. Now, Alex says GPT‑6 Astra reduces the work needed to bring those ideas into the product.

With less friction between prototyping and production, Alex claims Higgsfield AI can develop and ship better products faster.

Next, Higgsfield AI wants creators to be able to describe an idea and see it take shape as they talk. Alex calls that vision “voice to movie,” with AI understanding a creator’s spoken intention and rendering their vision in real time.

He sees OpenAI’s advances in planning, tool calling, image generation, and voice bringing that experience closer. He describes its voice model as “best in class for voice understanding and just for regular communication.”.

For Higgsfield AI, the ambition is to make creating a film feel more like describing an idea, with AI handling more of the work in between.

Latest Update: The EU’s next chapter in AI is agentic

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 2 min read (425 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~2 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • According to recent reports, across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools.
  • We have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents a substantial share of activity⁠.
  • This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated consumers.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

According to recent reports, across the EU, businesses are expanding how they use AI through agentic tools. People are moving beyond asking questions to using agents to carry out tasks from planning through completion. Our latest report from OpenAI Economic Research examines how agentic use is growing across enterprises and small businesses, focusing on differences in usage intensity and the kinds of work people do with ChatGPT.

We have found that, among ChatGPT Enterprise customers, agentic use already represents a substantial share of activity⁠. In our EU sample, Codex and ChatGPT Work now account for more than half of output tokens.

This analysis defines small or medium businesses as businesses with 200 or fewer associated consumers.

Recent findings suggest that the agentic shift extends to small and medium businesses. Since May 2026, weekly active owners of Codex and ChatGPT Work among EU small and medium businesses grew more than eightfold, with growth across every member state.

It has been revealed that but we also found that the EU’s adoption of agentic AI is far from uniform. Among the ChatGPT Enterprise accounts in our sample, the share of output tokens generated through Codex and ChatGPT Work ranged from 22% in Slovenia to 85% in Lithuania. The differences across countries extends beyond the intensity of agentic use. The kinds of work people bring to ChatGPT also vary across countries.

Industry observers note that frontier firms are defined as the top 10% of firms by output tokens per active user. Sample includes only ChatGPT Enterprise and Business accounts.

In a recent development, the takeaway is that EU frontier firms use AI much more intensively than typical EU firms, but still trail firms at the global frontier. In September, frontier firms in the EU generated more than four times as many output tokens per active user as typical EU firms. Even so, frontier firms outside the EU generated more than twice as many output tokens per active user as frontier EU firms. EU-based firms also represented only 10% of the frontier firms globally, which is low considering that the EU accounts for a higher share of registered companies globally⁠(opens in a fresh window).

These figures reveal a substantial gap in how intensively businesses use AI. As agentic capabilities advance, the EU’s opportunity is to turn broader adoption into deeper use, stronger businesses, higher productivity and meaningful benefits for workers. Closing that gap means helping businesses move beyond experimentation, giving workers the skills and confidence to use AI, and making advanced capabilities more accessible and affordable.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

Sample-Aware Test-Time Adaptation for Medical Image-to-Image Translation

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (189 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2508.00766v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Image-to-image translation has emerged as a powerful technique in medical imaging, enabling tasks such as image denoising and cross-modality conversion. However, it suffers from limitations in handling out-of-distribution samples without causing performance degradation. To address this limitation, we propose a novel Test-Time Adaptation (TTA) framework that dynamically adjusts the translation process based on the characteristics of each test sample. Our method introduces a Reconstruction Module to quantify the domain shift and a Dynamic Adaptation Block that selectively modifies the internal features of a pretrained translation model to mitigate the shift without compromising the performance on in-distribution samples that do not require adaptation. We evaluate our approach on two medical image-to-image translation tasks: low-dose CT denoising and T1 to T2 MRI translation, showing consistent improvements over both the baseline translation model without TTA and prior TTA methods. Our analysis highlights the limitations of the state-of-the-art that uniformly apply the adaptation to both out-of-distribution and in-distribution samples, demonstrating that dynamic, sample-specific adjustment offers a promising path to improve model resilience in real-world scenarios. The code is available at: https://github.com/Sample-Aware-TTA/Code.

#39309. AIR: Rethinking Image-Text Offset Alignment in Multimodal Contrastive Representation Space

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (243 w)
📖 Baca
General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

AIR: Rethinking Image-Text Offset Alignment in Multimodal Contrastive Representation Space

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (243 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2506.10895v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Image-text offset alignment, which refers to the consistency between visual transformation directions and their corresponding textual transformation directions, has become an crucial relational property in multimodal contrastive representation spaces such as CLIP and SigLIP. This property plays a central role in text-driven visual transformation tasks, including generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing, where textual offsets are used to guide visual transformations. These methods fundamentally rely on the assumption that image and text offsets are well aligned, such that textual transformation directions can provide reliable guidance for corresponding visual transformations. However, the validity of this alignment assumption has not been systematically examined. In this work, we question this foundational assumption by conducting a comprehensive empirical analysis of image-text offset alignment in multimodal contrastive representation space. Our findings reveal not only noticeable offset misalignment but also a meaningful positive correlation between image-text offset misalignment and semantic concept distance across six large datasets and eight contrastive vision-language models. Based on this discovery, we propose Adaptation with Iterative Refinement (AIR), a method that iteratively refines text offsets through anchor sampling and our proposed concept description learning to mitigate the downstream effect of image-text offset misalignment and improve guidance accuracy. Comprehensive experiments on zero-shot generative model domain adaptation and text-guided object-centric image editing across 40 setups, including qualitative, quantitative, and user studies, consistently show that AIR enables state-of-the-art performance in these tasks.

Tech Report: How Block is building AI-powered security with OpenAI technology

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1021 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work.
  • Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.
  • Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

Block is using AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak to compress the time to fix vulnerabilities, freeing its security team to focus on strategic work.

Hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.

Minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch.

Analyst-hours per quarter handed back.

Analyst-hours of investigation completed each quarter.

In a recent development, at Block, the firm behind Square, Cash App, and Afterpay, the security team leverages the OpenAI Defense Factory: where AI handles vulnerability discovery, detection, and response at a scale that no human team could keep up with. With AI systems including OpenAI Daybreak, Block is taking just hours to do work that used to take weeks.

Block’s security team has been focused on responsibly adopting AI across workflows, whether that’s code generation or security operations. “What it’s really centered on is having a new teammate that you can scale with,” James Nettesheim, Chief Information Security Officer, says. “It’s not like a more traditional automation where you had to go step by step. You can prompt it with a fairly bespoke, ambiguous problem and work through it together.”.

Projects like reviewing a software bug or parsing a log would take days or weeks to complete. Now the team can complete those projects in a fraction of the time, with a human still validating every result.

It has been revealed that for example, for detection tuning, every investigation stores its raw query evidence, so the team can now replay a proposed detection change against seven months of production telemetry in under an hour. That work used to mean requerying hundreds of old cases by hand, and often it rarely happened in practice since it was so time-consuming.

It has been revealed that the team has also gotten more particular about which model they’re using for which job. “We used to use the latest model, but you don’t need to do that anymore,” he says. “It’s been a learning experience to choose different models for different tasks.” Block’s security harness is built on top of Daybreak to help route tasks to the right model, and it includes hooks for humans to take over tasks or for agents to verify each other’s work. The team continually evaluates these systems against internal benchmarks and real-world performance, adjusting its approach when needed, including routing work to human review when that is the responsible path.

The automated triage system has resulted in faster work (and more of it) getting done. Block’s security team has seen a 50% boost to triage throughput, a 50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations, and an entirely new autonomous hunting capability. Nettesheim claims, “This performs ~1,100 analyst-hours of investigation per quarter, because every alert now gets a full, deep investigation across all elements the alert involves. Our system works every alert like it’s the only alert we’ve got that day.”.

Traditional scanning tools flag a single vulnerability in isolation, but Block’s security team can go much further with Daybreak. The model helps hypothesize about attack patterns and chain together a series of attacks into a full end-to-end compromise path, surfacing vulnerabilities that might have existed for years.

According to recent reports, in one case, an alert on a single laptop looked like a minor policy issue on its own. But during peer review, the model followed an indicator that appeared only incidentally in the evidence, joined it against Block’s identity logs, and surfaced a much larger set of issues. “One routine endpoint alert became a campaign takedown. No single tool makes that join. The signal only exists across two products’ logs,” James claims.

In a recent development, another example when Daybreak helped was during a recent red team exercise. The model was given a few hints about an internal system, and it chained together a full attack path—SQL injection, privilege escalation, a foothold, credential enumeration, and a pivot to other systems—in about two hours. This would typically take a human red teamer several days. In recent red team exercises, the time from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch was 18 minutes.

Finding the vulnerabilities is only as good as the ability to fix them. Nettesheim walks through the process his team uses on every finding: locate where the concern lives in the code and identify who owns it, then move to remediation. “You propose a patch, you confirm exploitability, and then you verify that you have fixed it, with a human in the loop guiding it and deploying the code changes.”.

It has been revealed that while agents are technically capable, they don’t carry an organization’s context or the reasoning behind previous decisions. A human provides that context and strategy, and that’s where his team comes in to provide a human layer of review. As AI’s judgment is proven out in practice, Nettesheim states, “we’ll slowly ladder up the risk level to use it for more sensitive systems.”.

Less than one hour to replay a proposed detection change against seven months of telemetry.

18 minutes from submitting a high-level vulnerability to an automated proposed patch in recent red team exercises.

Roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter of false-positive triage handed back.

Approximately 1,100 analyst-hours of investigation completed per quarter.

50% boost to triage throughput.

50% increase in intelligence gathering and investigations.

It has been revealed that detection and response work alone has handed back roughly 600 analyst-hours per quarter that used to go toward triaging false positives. With that time back, the team now spends more time on deeper investigations and building more automation responsibly.

As the pace of attack increases and AI models keep advancing, Nettesheim sees an opportunity to reduce the number of vulnerabilities introduced in the first place. That would free security teams to spend less time patching and more time on preventative, strategic work.

“OpenAI is shifting the advantage to defenders by putting these advanced capabilities in everyone’s hands,” he says. “It’s typically only been in very high-profile technology companies and government hands. But everyone, including critical infrastructure, schools, small businesses, can now start utilizing this technology to defend their networks.”.

#39302. How Third Moment Research runs 10,000 agents for 36+ hours

📅 14 Oct 2026 • ⏱️ 5m • 📚 Deep Dive (1063 w)

How Third Moment Research runs 10,000 agents for 36+ hours

📅 14 Oct 2026 | ⏱️ 5 min read (1063 words, 📚 Deep Dive) | Source: Openai

⏱️ ~5 mins left to finish
📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.
  • In a recent development, every manufacturer has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success.
  • The company is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With GPT‑6 Astra and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Codex, and Daybreak for cybersecurity, this AI lab builds agents that focus for days and improve with use.

Hours per autonomous research session.

Reduction in backtest time with Codex.

Trillion OpenAI tokens in a single day.

In a recent development, every manufacturer has its own workflows, tools, edge cases, and definitions of success. ⁠(opens in a newly introduced window)Third Moment Research⁠(opens in a new window) believes the best agents should be really good at that specific work and should improve their capabilities the more they’re used.

The company is building a self-improving AI system around that idea, using OpenAI’s latest models to understand agent behavior, identify recurring weaknesses, and automatically create thousands of synthetic scenarios around those problems. The team uses those scenarios to improve agents, repeating the process as new challenges emerge.

According to recent reports, codex, GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol support the system’s research and computational work, enabling Third Moment to run 10,000 agents at once on investigations lasting 36-48 hours. The manufacturer also uses Daybreak to test the security of the environments where agents work.

It has been revealed that one of Third Moment’s early applications is in the field of quantitative finance given the clear measure of success. This domain provides a concrete setting to study how agents work and where they struggle. The team uses Codex to find and address problems in the research environment.

In one instance, it used Codex with GPT‑5.6, the latest GPT model at the time, to analyze thousands of recorded simulation trajectories (the agents’ actions and the environment’s responses) alongside timestamps and the codebase.

Codex uncovered a bottleneck: backtesting a trading strategy across a year of order-level US equity data took several hours. While waiting, agents repeatedly polled for completion, wasting tokens and filling their context with status checks.

Recent findings suggest that after profiling the backtest and analyzing its inputs and usage, Codex identified a caching optimization and a memory-packing technique. It experimented with solutions and deployed the fix to production, reducing the backtest from approximately 3 hours to approximately 3 to 5 minutes. This reduced token use and context pollution, freeing more of the agents’ token budget for further experiments.

Third Moment gives each agent the tools, information, and environment it needs for a specific job. For quantitative research, the team runs the default Codex harness inside a Dockerized environment. Agents receive a terabyte of data, documentation, and a research repository with modules for feature engineering, GPU-supported model training, trading strategies, and simulation.

GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol provide the reasoning, while the Codex harness gives agents tools to act, create looks, set objectives, spawn subagents, and compact context as work continues.

To address agents that stop before completing a task, Third Moment treats Codex as a subagent within an outer harness powered by GPT‑6 Sol or GPT‑6.1 Sol. The outer harness examines the trajectory when a task is left unfinished and determines whether to retry, terminate the job, or escalate to human review.

It has been revealed that in that research environment, agents work to improve a baseline trading system built by Third Moment’s engineers. They test trading strategies on historical data, assess whether an improvement is meaningful or noise, and use each result to choose the next experiment. According to Adam, their work has improved the baseline trading system.

Before GPT‑5.5, Adam claims models could only execute experiments prescribed by a user. With GPT‑5.5 and GPT‑5.6, models working with the Codex harness could use results to design follow-up experiments. Now with GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, agents can investigate root causes through hundreds of experiments running in parallel with subagents.

That progression has helped agents explore research directions the team hadn’t anticipated. In one session, GPT‑6.1 Sol identified the impact of non-displayed trades on an exchange where those trades accounted for an unexpectedly large share of volume. “This was an unobvious result that our research team did not initially consider,” indicates Adam.

In a recent development, third Moment evaluates models across optimization, machine learning systems, and quantitative research. It tests frontier releases at their highest reasoning settings, assessing their ability to navigate repositories, write efficient code, and sustain an investigation. Current testing also includes GPT‑6 Luna.

One benchmark asks agents to reduce a live scoreboard service’s patch latency while preserving its outputs. The team measures speedup by dividing the average runtime of an expert-crafted solution by that of the model’s solution on the same hardware, subject to correctness. GPT‑6 Astra delivered the biggest speedup, according to Adam.

For targeted work, including checks for specific security weaknesses in the simulation system, the team uses more efficient models like GPT‑5.6 Terra. For deep research, Adam believes stronger reasoning can justify higher cost: “In the space of quantitative finance, the value of finding some interesting signal is extremely high.”.

With 10,000 agents running autonomously, Third Moment needs a way to test the security of its research environments at scale. The team uses the Daybreak cybersecurity platform to automate that testing before simulations launch.

The tests check whether an agent could break out of its research environment and access the wider network. “By using Daybreak, we’re able to have agents themselves do penetration testing on the simulation and test the infrastructure and security of it,” says Adam.

Sources indicate that third Moment’s ambition extends to the specialized work companies do every day. For a retailer, that could mean making better supply chain decisions when inventory is short or a supplier is delayed. For an engineering team, it could mean finding performance bottlenecks in a large codebase. For a document-heavy business, it could mean identifying where commitments in one document don’t match outcomes recorded in another.

Building on the reasoning capabilities of GPT‑6 Astra, GPT‑6 Sol, and GPT‑6.1 Sol, Third Moment intends to expand from individual investigations to hundreds of thousands of collaborating subagents. Its roadmap calls for trillions of tokens supporting chains of dozens of dependent experiments, with the goal of using that research to autonomously improve agents as upcoming challenges arise.

For Adam, this would give people more capacity to shape how agents learn and work: “Humans can be in a much more leveraged position, where they can think about how to do research and optimize the research itself instead of actually doing the research.”.

General ⚖️ Neutral 🌐 Arxiv ↗ Open Full Page

TRIM: Achieving Extreme Sparsity with Targeted Row-wise Iterative Metric-driven Pruning

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (153 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2505.16743v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Large language models (LLMs) present substantial computational and memory challenges. Existing one-shot pruning methods often use a uniform sparsity target for all rows within a layer, which can be too coarse at high sparsity. This work introduces TRIM (Targeted Row-wise Iterative Metric-driven pruning), a forward-statistics-based wrapper that allocates different sparsity ratios to individual output rows while keeping model weights frozen. TRIM separates the choice of which weights to prune (scoring) from how many to prune in each row (allocation), and composes with existing scorers and layer-wise allocations. Across Qwen2.5, LLaMA-2, and OPT models, its largest gains occur at 70-80% sparsity. At 80%, adding TRIM to OWL reduces WikiText-2 perplexity from 348.48 to 180.67 for Qwen2.5-14B and from 6461.43 to 324.14 for OPT-13B. We conclude that fine-grained, row-wise allocation is an effective mechanism for substantially improving one-shot pruning quality in the extreme-sparsity regime. Code: https://github.com/flobk/TRIM.

Latest Update: VFRTok: Variable Frame Rates Video Tokenizer with Duration-Proportional Information Assumption

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (176 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

arXiv:2505.12053v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Modern video generation frameworks based on Latent Diffusion Models suffer from inefficiencies in tokenization due to the Frame-Proportional Information Assumption. Existing tokenizers provide fixed temporal compression rates, causing the computational cost of the diffusion model to scale linearly with the frame rate. The paper proposes the Duration-Proportional Information Assumption: the upper bound on the information capacity of a video is proportional to the duration rather than the number of frames. Based on this insight, the paper introduces VFRTok, a Transformer-based video tokenizer, that enables variable frame rate encoding and decoding through asymmetric frame rate training between the encoder and decoder. Furthermore, the paper proposes Partial Rotary Position Embeddings (RoPE) to decouple position and content modeling, which groups correlated patches into unified tokens. The Partial RoPE effectively improves content-awareness, enhancing the video generation capability. Benefiting from the compact and continuous spatio-temporal representation, VFRTok achieves competitive reconstruction quality and state-of-the-art generation fidelity while using only 1/8 tokens compared to existing tokenizers. The code and weights are released at: https://github.com/KwaiVGI/VFRTok.

SentinelOne cuts malware analysis from weeks to hours

📖 0% read
💡 Key Takeaways
  • With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.
  • Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks.
  • According to recent reports, reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

With OpenAI Daybreak, SentinelOne cuts weeks of malware analysis to hours, creating capacity to investigate more threats.

Hours to reverse-engineer malware, down from 4–6 weeks.

According to recent reports, reverse engineering a sophisticated piece of malware can take a top security researcher four to six weeks. It’s painstaking work where researchers pull apart software to understand how it behaves, often retracing their steps as they uncover newly introduced information. Gregor Stewart, Chief AI Officer at SentinelOne, states OpenAI Daybreak can now produce human-level reverse-engineering output in roughly eight hours.

Industry observers note that by reducing the time needed for deep analysis, OpenAI gives SentinelOne’s researchers room to investigate more malware and connect findings across samples. That wider view often reveals relationships that isolated investigations might miss. Stewart describes the opportunity as “a kind of intelligence that we were never able to afford before.”.

Daybreak gives defenders access to OpenAI models for cybersecurity work. SentinelOne uses these capabilities to reverse engineer malware, examining software to understand how it behaves. Faster analysis gives its researchers more capacity to investigate additional samples.

Stewart emphasizes that his team remains responsible for the outcome. “The only thing that can’t be automated is accountability,” he indicates. “Take a decision to change the architecture. This is something that still you would want human eyes on, whereas point fixes or things that don’t fundamentally change the way the software works, those might be better suited for automation,” he adds.

Sources indicate that historically, research teams at SentinelOne had to reserve deep investigation for the most interesting or important threats they uncovered. “We were only able to reverse very small numbers of pieces of software,” Stewart says. With fewer samples to compare, they had fewer opportunities to spot connections between threats.

Recent findings suggest that faster analysis with Daybreak gives researchers more opportunities to compare malware samples and look for shared components. For example, a component found in two apparently unrelated samples could give researchers a lead to pursue during a customer investigation.

Comparing findings across more samples also reveals broader relationships between threats. Seeing those relationships, Stewart notes, “would help you defend further out, and be more proactive about your defense.”.

Within SentinelOne, Stewart states access to OpenAI’s cyber capabilities is allowing more people to take responsibility for security work. “Almost everyone now has access to the kind of expertise that was in very short supply until maybe even a few months ago,” he says. More team members can investigate problems themselves rather than relying on a small group of specialists.

Stewart wants to bring OpenAI’s cyber capabilities into code creation, so SentinelOne developers can address security issues as they build.

📅 26 Nov 2026 • ⏱️ 1m • 📖 Standard (215 w)

Latest Update: Causal pieces: analysing and improving spiking neural networks piece by piece

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (215 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

In a recent development, arXiv:2504.14015v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: We introduce "causal pieces", a novel concept for analysing spiking neural networks (SNNs), inspired by "linear pieces" used to study expressivity and trainability in artificial neural networks (ANNs). Causal pieces partition the input and parameter space of a feedforward SNN with single-spike coding into distinct regions where the same subnetwork causes the output spikes. For networks of current-based leaky integrate-and-fire (LIF) neurons with large membrane time constants, we show that within each causal piece, output spike times are locally Lipschitz continuous with respect to inputs and network parameters. We further prove a lower bound on the approximation error that depends on the number of causal pieces. Thus, the number of causal pieces is a measure of the approximation capabilities of SNNs, which is valid despite spike-time discontinuities and applies to networks with both excitatory and inhibitory synapses. Empirically, we find that parameter initialisations yielding more causal pieces on the training set strongly correlate with SNN training success across multiple benchmarks, including Yin-Yang, Fashion-MNIST, and EuroSAT. Moreover, simulations with standard single-spike LIF neurons indicate that our findings extend beyond the theoretically analysed regime. These results establish causal pieces as a powerful and principled tool for analysing and improving the computational capabilities of SNNs.

Mamba-3D as Masked Autoencoders for Accurate and Data-Efficient Analysis of Medical Ultrasound Videos

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (175 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

According to recent reports, arXiv:2503.20258v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Ultrasound videos are an notable form of clinical imaging data, and deep learning-based automated analysis can improve diagnostic accuracy and clinical efficiency. However, the scarcity of labeled data and the inherent challenges of video analysis have impeded the advancement of related methods. In this work, we introduce E-ViM$^3$, a data-efficient Vision Mamba network that preserves the 3D structure of video data, enhancing long-range dependencies and inductive biases to better model space-time correlations. With our design of Enclosure Global Tokens (EGT), the model captures and aggregates global features more effectively than competing methods. To further improve data efficiency, we employ masked video modeling for self-supervised pre-training, with the proposed Spatial-Temporal Chained (STC) masking strategy designed to adapt to various video scenarios. Experiments demonstrate that E-ViM$^3$ performs as the state-of-the-art in two high-level semantic analysis tasks across four datasets of varying sizes: EchoNet-Dynamic, CAMUS, MICCAI-BUV, and WHBUS. Furthermore, our model achieves competitive performance with limited labels, highlighting its potential impact on real-world clinical applications.

📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

See how Amp pushes the frontier of what agents can do with GPT‑6 Astra, Ultrafast, GPT‑Live‑1, and Sign in with ChatGPT.

Amp⁠(opens in a upcoming window) is building a frontier AI agent that helps developers turn ambitious ideas into working software. For Quinn Slack, Amp’s CEO, each improvement in the models is an opportunity to expand what the agent can do, from helping developers decide what to build to writing code and designing pages.

Sources indicate that amp chooses and recommends models based on what works best for its users, and OpenAI models account for the majority of tokens used in Amp. Quinn shares, “OpenAI is very transparent, and when there are safeguards applied, users know and they understand. That makes it really easy to use OpenAI models. You can do all of your work in Amp with OpenAI models and be really happy.”.

As builders give agents more work, token costs can become a constraint. Quinn describes some Amp people consuming 10 billion tokens a week. He believes that if people watch every increment of usage, it might hold them back from finding out what an agent is capable of.

To help alleviate that, Amp launched its Sign in with ChatGPT integration. Quinn notes it gives Amp users access to more tokens and OpenAI models, including GPT‑6 Astra, which changes how willing they are to let an agent take on a larger task.

“Sign in with ChatGPT means that people can have that feeling where they’re not counting every single token,” he states. “And once you actually let the agent go and have a longer leash, then you realize just how much it can do.” Quinn says he sees people using the agent to blueprint, decide what to build, and continue working after they ship.

It has been revealed that amp wants agents to help with all the work that goes into building and growing a product. Its own 20-person team uses them that way, including in marketing. “We don’t have someone devoted to it, but we have an agent devoted to it,” Quinn states. The team relies on the agent to improve the experience for fresh people and help more people discover Amp through search and other channels.

In a recent development, for that work, having high-quality writing and design is critical. GPT‑6 Astra helps the team produce documentation and design pages that meet Amp’s exacting standards.

Quinn’s experiments with GPT‑6 Astra continue at home. He gave it the aims for his house and used it to create a 3D model in Blender. He and his children then turn that model into games: adding a lazy river through the house or chasing garlic around it, inspired by their grandmother’s dislike of garlic. “And that was not possible just a couple months ago,” he indicates.

According to recent reports, amp recently declared Puck, a conversational AI assistant built into Amp that helps users launch and manage other agents. Users can ask Puck to start an agent to investigate a bug, coordinate several agents, or find a previous conversation about a technical problem.

With Calling Puck, powered by GPT‑Live‑1, customers can talk to Puck in real time, including from a watch. Quinn imagines people using it to keep their agents working while they’re away from their computers, even while out for a run.

Amp has been testing Ultrafast mode with GPT‑6 Astra, and Quinn indicates the greater speed changes how people use agents. Today, people often switch between several agent tasks while waiting for each to finish. Faster responses could let people juggle fewer agents, or give agents more time to check their own work before returning a result.

For Amp, the next step is to bring more of the work before and after coding into the agent, so builders can carry an idea further without handling every step themselves. “There’s this unknown of what humans will create, and that’s what we all get to see. It’s cool to be playing a part in that,” Quinn says.

Tech Report: On the Efficiency of Structured Pruning in Small Language Model Pretraining

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (251 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

⏱️ ~1 mins left to finish
📖 0% read

Sources indicate that arXiv:2503.05920v2 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Companies that deploy generative language models on edge devices often need to train small models from scratch due to legal, data-governance, or product-customization requirements. An alternative approach is to train an enlarged model and compress it to the target size via structured pruning, but this advantage becomes unclear once the cost of pretraining the enlarged model is included. We introduce the enlarge-and-prune framework to study this question under full-cost accounting, and show that conventional enlarge-and-prune pipelines -- which train the enlarged model, prune it, and recover in separate stages -- do not consistently outperform direct small-model training under the same total token budget. To overcome this limitation, we propose IDEA Prune, an integrated enlarge-and-prune pipeline that unifies enlarged model pretraining, iterative structured pruning, and recovery under a single cosine annealing learning rate schedule. In controlled experiments compressing 2.8B models to 1.3B with up to 2T tokens on the same dataset, IDEA Prune consistently outperforms conventional pipelines and modestly improves overall performance relative to the scratch baseline, improving MMLU accuracy to 46.4%, compared with 31.4-33.4% for conventional pipelines. These advantages are preserved after downstream supervised fine-tuning, where IDEA Prune matches or outperforms all baselines of the same size on instruction following, math reasoning, and code generation. Our analysis further reveals that intermediate checkpoints provide more favorable pruning starting points than fully converged ones, and that an enlargement factor of approximately 2.6x yields the best pruned models in the tested regime.

📅 26 Nov 2026 | ⏱️ 1 min read (184 words, 📖 Standard) | Source: Arxiv

arXiv:2411.14062v3 Announce Type: replace-cross Abstract: Existing benchmarks often rely on predefined questions or reference captions, limiting their flexibility for evaluating detailed descriptions on new image collections. We present MMGenBench, an automated benchmark framework for evaluating Large Multimodal Models (LMMs) from raw images without per-image questions or reference captions. The pipeline generates descriptions, reconstructs images with a frozen text-to-image model, and compares the original and reconstructed images using a frozen image encoder. It produces reusable per-image scores and inspectable reconstructions, supporting both model comparison and diagnosis of reconstructible visual information. We construct MMGenBench-Domain with 10,000 generated images and MMGenBench-Test with 1,284 images spanning 13 overlapping visual patterns. Evaluation of 68 LMMs reveals pattern-specific differences in reconstruction quality that overall scores can obscure. On 1,000 human-labeled caption pairs from six models, the default score achieves 90.00\% sample-level agreement. Factual perturbations and component analyses characterize the score's sensitivity under the evaluated pipeline, while a COCO study provides initial validation on natural photographs. MMGenBench complements existing benchmarks by linking automated comparisons to visual evidence of the information preserved in LMM descriptions. Project page: https://github.com/lerogo/MMGenBench.

💡 Key Takeaways

  • Recent findings suggest that for lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities.
  • Recent findings suggest that though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage.
📑 Quick Jump: 1. Overview • 2. Key Details • 3. Closing Notes

In collaboration with OpenAI, Sullivan & Cromwell developed Agreement Analyzer, an AI tool for identifying issues in a draft agreement.

Recent findings suggest that for lawyers at Sullivan & Cromwell, reviewing a draft agreement includes weighing its terms against relevant precedents, using approaches based on the Firm’s experience and being mindful of a client’s priorities. The firm’s Agreement Analyzer brings those inputs into a single review workflow, producing analysis and proposed changes that lawyers can inspect and refine.

Recent findings suggest that though AI was initially used most for repetitive, administrative tasks like drafting email responses or checking calendars, Savva finds that recent improvements in AI models’ analytical capabilities have changed its usage. “Now, we’re seeing many more opportunities for use in challenging legal tasks such as deep analysis of complex agreements,” he claims.

Agreement Analyzer helps lawyers compare corresponding provisions across precedents and track how those provisions interact.

Sources indicate that sullivan & Cromwell partner John Savva developed Agreement Analyzer as a single-user proof of concept built with Codex. He then collaborated with OpenAI on improving the quality of outputs, enhancing efficiency through parallel processing and transforming the application into a tool that could be used by multiple lawyers at the same time.

Agreement Analyzer integrates Sullivan & Cromwell’s workflows, curated firm precedents, negotiating playbooks and ChatGPT Enterprise. After inputting a draft agreement into the tool, a lawyer can add their own selected precedents and a playbook with firm and client positions, as well as information on market practice. The tool performs multiple review cycles from different perspectives, synthesizes the outputs, helps identify potential issues and returns a memorandum and proposed tracked changes for a lawyer to review, adapt or reject.

Industry observers note that savva emphasizes that what makes an AI tool’s output trustworthy is full transparency. “If an AI tool makes a claim about market practice, you need to be able to see the source of that information,” he says.

In a recent development, savva describes an application in which agents develop conclusions and other agents challenge them in an adversarial process. In a potential use case, specialized agents review the agreement in parallel for such things as market deviations and risk allocation, interactions between clauses, and ambiguities that could impact litigation. The results distinguish findings supported after challenge by other agents, dismissed findings, and unverified issues retained with qualifications. Lawyers can inspect the issues, their supporting explanations, and the relevant precedents, then decide which findings warrant changes in the final markup.

Sullivan & Cromwell is continuing to explore tools shaped around specific legal tasks. For Savva, stronger analytical capabilities create an opportunity to support more of the research and writing process.

Savva points to advances in reasoning capabilities with GPT‑6 Astra: “Astra’s really moved things forward in terms of the quality of the reasoning that’s available, and that has been the bottleneck in the past,” he says.
